questions.stem: What do we call an animal or plant that has died out everywhere on Earth?
options: endangered
extinct
protected
migrating
questions.explanation: Extinct means no longer living anywhere on Earth, and it can never come back. Endangered means in danger of becoming extinct.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Cutting down forests is called ___. Harmful things put into the air or water are called ___.
questions.explanation: Deforestation destroys the homes of animals such as elephants. Pollution includes smoke, rubbish, plastic and dirty water.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Match each way of caring for the environment to an example.
pairs: take a cloth bag to the market
use an old tin as a pencil pot
take newspapers to the paper collector (bhangari)
switch off lights and fans when you leave a room
questions.explanation: Reduce means use less, reuse means use again, and recycle means make used materials into new things. Saving energy and not littering help too.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Sort these actions into those that help the environment and those that harm it.
questions.explanation: Planting trees, using cloth bags and cleaning up help living things. Plastic in rivers, hunting and wasting electricity cause harm.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: There are far more people in Bangladesh today than long ago, so our actions can have a bigger effect on living things.
questions.explanation: Today there are more than 170 million people in Bangladesh. We use more land, water and wood, so what we do matters more.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Which of these harm the environment? Choose all that are right.
options: filling in wetlands to build roads
pouring dirty factory water into rivers
planting trees in the monsoon
catching too many young fish
making a national park
questions.explanation: Filling wetlands, polluting rivers and overfishing harm living things. Planting trees and making national parks protect them.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Why is it a problem to catch too many young fish?
options: Fishing nets get damaged.
The remaining fish grow too large.
Young fish are too small to taste good.
Not enough fish grow up to breed.
questions.explanation: Young fish that are caught cannot grow up and have babies, so the number of fish falls. Laws protect fish while they breed.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how plastic litter can harm a sea animal.
sequence: A plastic bag is dropped on the street.
Rain washes it into a drain.
The drain carries it to a river and then the sea.
A turtle mistakes it for food and eats it.
questions.explanation: Plastic does not rot, so litter flows from drains to rivers and the sea, where turtles and dolphins can mistake it for food.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Before 2002, many thin plastic bags were used in Dhaka. What problems did they cause?
questions.model_answer: The thin plastic bags blocked the drains, and this made floods worse.
questions.explanation: Plastic does not rot. Thin plastic bags blocked drains and made floods worse in Dhaka, so Bangladesh banned them in 2002.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: A plastic bottle left on the ground can take how long to break down?
options: hundreds of years
about one whole year
only a few weeks
around ten years
questions.explanation: Plastic breaks down very slowly, so one bottle can stay in the environment for hundreds of years.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: The Sundarbans is protected as a wildlife ___, where animals can live safely.
questions.explanation: National parks and wildlife sanctuaries such as the Sundarbans and Lawachara protect habitats.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: In Bangladesh, people plant millions of trees every year during the ___.
questions.explanation: Planting trees during the wet monsoon helps them grow. Trees give homes and food to animals and help to protect the soil.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Taking a cloth bag to the market is an example of recycling.
questions.explanation: Taking a cloth bag means you use fewer plastic bags, so it is an example of reducing. Recycling means making used materials into new things.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Which action saves electricity at home?
options: leaving the light on in an empty room
keeping the television on all day
switching off the fan when you leave
running the fan with nobody in the room
questions.explanation: Switching off lights and fans when you leave a room uses less electricity.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Why is it important to tell other people about caring for the environment?
questions.model_answer: Many people acting together make a much bigger difference than one person.
questions.explanation: One person can make a difference, but many people together can make a big difference. You can talk to your family or start an eco-club.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Which picture shows a way to **help** the environment?
questions.explanation: A reusable bag lets you use fewer plastic bags. Factory smoke, car exhaust and oil spills pollute the air and water.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Sort these pictures into things that help the environment and things that harm it.
questions.explanation: Recycling, reusable bags, planting and putting litter in bins help. Smoke, oil spills and exhaust fumes pollute.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Match each picture to what it does.
pairs: makes used materials into new things
questions.explanation: Pollution harms living things. Planting trees and recycling help them.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Plastic in rivers flows to the sea. Which of these animals can mistake plastic for food? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Turtles and dolphins live in the sea and can mistake floating plastic for food. Deer and parrots do not live in the sea.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Cutting down forests destroys the homes of animals such as elephants. Which picture shows an animal that loses its home?
questions.explanation: Elephants live in forests, so they lose their food and shelter when forests are cut down. Whales, sharks and goldfish live in water.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: At break time, Nadia sees sweet wrappers all over the school playground. What is the best action?
options: Sweep them into the nearest drain with a broom.
Wear gloves, pick them up and put them in a bin.
Leave them where they are for the wind to blow away.
Burn them in a pile behind the school building.
questions.explanation: Litter should go in a bin. Sweeping it into a drain blocks the drain and burning it pollutes the air. Gloves protect hands from dirt and sharp things.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: The class litter survey shows that sweet wrappers are the most common litter. Which action fits this evidence best?
options: Plant more trees near the school gate.
Make the playground a little bigger.
Put more bins next to the snack shop.
Stop the learners from drinking water.
questions.explanation: Good actions use the evidence. Wrappers come from snacks, so bins near the snack shop (or snacks without wrappers) would help most.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Tuli does a "rubbish diary" at home. Sort each action into reduce, reuse or recycle.
items: taking a water bottle from home instead of buying one
using a jar to store rice
taking newspapers to the bhangari collector
printing on both sides of the paper
giving old clothes to someone else
sending empty glass bottles to be made into new glass
questions.explanation: Reduce means use less. Reuse means use again. Recycle means turning used materials into new things.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Throwing plastic into a drain is harmless because the drain takes it far away.
questions.explanation: Plastic does not rot. It can block drains, cause floods, and end up in rivers and the sea where it harms animals.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: A new road will cross a wetland where fish, frogs and birds live. What is the best plan?
options: Cut down all the trees around the wetland.
Fill in the wetland quickly because it is only mud.
Build the road fast and tell nobody about it.
Look for a route that goes round the wetland.
questions.explanation: Filling in wetlands destroys the homes of fish, frogs and birds. A good plan protects the habitat and still meets people's needs.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Class 4A collected 42 pieces of litter: sweet wrappers 18, plastic bottles 7, paper 10, food waste 5, cans 2. Which statement is correct?
options: Paper and cans together were more than the wrappers alone.
Sweet wrappers were less than half of all the litter.
Plastic bottles were the second most common kind of litter.
There were 40 pieces of litter in all, counting everything.
questions.explanation: 18 is less than half of 42 (which is 21). Paper and cans make 12, which is fewer than 18. Paper (10) was second, and the total is 42.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: A family uses 5 thin plastic bags every week. They start using one strong jute bag every week instead. How many plastic bags do they avoid in a year of 52 weeks?
options: 52 bags
57 bags
260 bags
520 bags
questions.explanation: 5 × 52 = 260 plastic bags a year. One strong jute bag can be used again and again.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Give one way people have helped an ecosystem in Bangladesh and one way people have harmed one. Explain both.
questions.model_answer: Helped: protecting the Sundarbans as a sanctuary lets tigers and deer survive. Harmed: polluting the Buriganga killed fish and made the water unsafe.
questions.explanation: People help by protecting habitats, planting trees and making laws. People harm by polluting, cutting down forests, hunting and overfishing.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: Raju says: "Recycling means using something again, like using a jar to store rice." What is wrong with this?
options: That is reusing; recycling means making used materials into new things.
Recycling means using less of something every single day.
Nothing is wrong, because recycling just means using things again and again.
Recycling means throwing things away safely in the right bin.
questions.explanation: Using a jar again is reusing. Recycling changes used paper, glass, metal or plastic into new things.

questions.title: Humans and the Environment
questions.stem: A shopkeeper compares thin plastic bags and jute bags. Which statements are fair? Choose all that are right.
options: Jute bags rot away naturally in a few months.
Plastic bags are cheap and light.
Jute bags can be reused many times.
Plastic bags rot away in a few months.
Jute is made from oil.
questions.explanation: Plastic bags are cheap but last hundreds of years. Jute is a plant fibre that rots away and can be reused. Plastic, not jute, comes from oil.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Which sentence describes the **climate** of a place?
options: It is very windy at school this afternoon.
Tomorrow morning will be foggy in Dhaka.
Sylhet gets a lot of rain every year.
It rained heavily here all night last night.
questions.explanation: Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years. The other sentences describe the weather on one day, which can change in a few hours.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Sort these sentences into weather and climate.
items: It is very windy this afternoon.
Sylhet gets a lot of rain every year.
Bangladesh has a monsoon season every year.
Winters in Dhaka are cool and dry.
questions.explanation: Weather is what the air is like today or this week. Climate is the usual weather of a place, worked out from many years of measurements.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Climate is the usual weather of a place, worked out from many ___ of measurements.
questions.explanation: Climate is found by measuring the weather for many years, usually 30.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Match each weather instrument to what it measures.
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature in °C and a rain gauge measures rain in mm. The wind vane shows direction, the anemometer shows speed, and the barometer measures air pressure.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Match each season in Bangladesh to its months (about).
questions.explanation: Summer is very hot with sudden storms. The monsoon is warm and very wet. Winter is cool and dry with foggy mornings.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Weather and climate can change non-living things too: heavy rain can make rivers flood.
questions.explanation: Weather and climate affect living things (rice is planted when the monsoon rains come) and non-living things (rivers flood, and heat and rain slowly break up rocks and roads).

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Why is the air near the ceiling of a room warmer than the air near the floor?
options: Heat cannot reach the floor.
Warm air sinks to the floor.
The ceiling gives out heat.
Warm air rises to the ceiling.
questions.explanation: When air is warmed it spreads out, becomes lighter and rises. Cooler air stays lower down.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a sea breeze forms.
sequence: The Sun warms the land faster than the sea.
The warm air over the land rises.
Cooler air from the sea moves in to take its place.
This moving air is a sea breeze.
questions.explanation: Wind is moving air. On a sunny day the land warms faster than the water, warm air rises over the land and cool air blows in from the sea.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Which places are likely to be the warmest at noon? Choose all that are right.
options: a dark tin roof in direct sunshine
a dark road in direct sunshine
under a big shady tree
beside a pond in the shade
questions.explanation: It is warmest in direct sunshine, especially on dark surfaces. It is coolest in the shade of trees and near water.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: A thermometer for measuring the air temperature should be kept in the ___.
questions.explanation: In direct sunshine a thermometer shows the temperature of the sunshine, not of the air. Keep it in the shade, about 1.5 m above the ground.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: A thermometer left in direct sunshine shows the true temperature of the air.
questions.explanation: In direct sunshine the thermometer heats up and shows the temperature of the sunshine, not the air. It should be kept in the shade.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Why do many old houses in Bangladesh have small openings high up in the walls?
questions.model_answer: Warm air rises and escapes through the high openings, and cooler air comes in lower down, keeping the house cool.
questions.explanation: Warm air rises. The high openings let it out, and cooler air flows in lower down to take its place.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: What does a barometer measure?
options: rainfall
air pressure
wind direction
temperature
questions.explanation: A barometer measures air pressure. Falling pressure often means a storm is coming.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: White, puffy clouds in a blue sky usually mean…
options: fine weather
heavy rain is on the way
a storm is coming
a cyclone is near
questions.explanation: White, puffy clouds mean fine weather. Dark grey clouds hold more water and often bring rain.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Which clues can tell you that a storm may be coming? Choose all that are right.
options: the barometer is falling
tall dark clouds are growing
the wind changes direction
a clear blue sky with a few thin white clouds
calm air and no clouds at all
questions.explanation: Falling pressure, tall dark clouds and a change of wind direction can all mean the weather is about to change.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Look at the weather instruments. Match each letter to its name.
questions.image_alt: Five weather instruments lettered A to E.
questions.explanation: A is a thermometer, B a rain gauge, C a wind vane, D an anemometer and E a barometer.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Which letter shows the white, puffy cloud that usually comes with fine weather?
questions.image_alt: Cloud types lettered.
options: A
B
C
D
questions.explanation: A is a cumulus cloud: white and puffy, a sign of fine weather. D is a tall cumulonimbus that can bring thunderstorms.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Look at the clouds. Match each letter to the name of the cloud.
questions.image_alt: Cloud types lettered.
questions.explanation: Cumulus clouds are puffy, stratus clouds form flat grey layers, cirrus clouds are thin and wispy, and cumulonimbus clouds are tall and bring thunderstorms.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Look at the sea breeze picture. In the daytime, which way does the cool air move near the ground?
questions.image_alt: Daytime sea breeze: warm air rises over the land and cooler air moves in from the sea.
options: from the sea to the land
straight up into the sky
straight down into the sea
from the land to the sea
questions.explanation: The land warms faster than the sea, so warm air rises over the land and cooler air moves in from the sea to take its place.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Sort these weather pictures into fine weather and wet or stormy weather.
questions.explanation: A bright sun and a few small clouds mean fine weather. Rain clouds, thunder clouds and cyclones bring wet or stormy weather.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Rina's class sets up a weather station. Where should they keep the thermometer to measure the air temperature?
options: on the tin roof of the shed in the sun
in the shade, about 1.5 m above the ground
on the hot concrete in the sunshine
inside a closed cupboard
questions.explanation: The air temperature should be measured in the shade, away from heat from the ground and the Sun. A tin roof or concrete in the sun would read much too high.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: On a hot afternoon, Joy wants to cool her room. It has one window near the floor and one near the ceiling. What should she do?
options: Open only the low window.
Open only the high window.
Open both windows.
Close both windows.
questions.explanation: Cool air comes in through the low window and warm air rises out through the high window, so opening both keeps the air moving.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Tomorrow is Sports Day. This afternoon the barometer is falling, the wind has changed direction and tall dark clouds are growing. What is the best forecast?
options: Cold, foggy weather is likely.
Hot, dry and sunny weather is likely.
Calm, clear weather is likely.
A storm with heavy rain is likely.
questions.explanation: Falling pressure, a change of wind direction and tall dark (cumulonimbus) clouds are signs of a storm.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: A haor farmer hears a flash flood warning on the radio. It is better to wait until the rice is completely ripe before harvesting.
questions.explanation: Slightly unripe rice still gives some food and money, but a flash flood would destroy all of it. Farmers should harvest early.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Why do farmers in Bangladesh plant rice when the monsoon rains arrive?
options: Rice needs a lot of water to grow.
Rice grows best in cold dry weather.
Rain keeps birds away from the rice.
The monsoon makes the soil harder.
questions.explanation: Weather and climate affect living things. The monsoon brings the water that rice plants need.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Class 4A measured the rainfall each morning for five days: 0 mm, 2 mm, 10 mm, 25 mm and 30 mm. What was the total rainfall?
options: 57 mm
67 mm
77 mm
87 mm

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Class 4A recorded the weather at 9 a.m. in June. Rain (mm): Sun 0, Mon 2, Tue 10, Wed 25, Thu 30. Pressure: steady, falling, falling, falling, low. On Thursday the clouds were dark and tall and the wind blew from the south-east, from the sea. Which forecast for Friday is best supported?
options: Dry and sunny, because Sunday was dry.
Dry, because the wind comes from the sea.
Wet again, because the rain is increasing and the pressure is low.
Cold and snowy, because the temperature is falling.
questions.explanation: A forecast uses trends. Rainfall has gone up every day, the pressure is low and the clouds are dark and tall, so more rain is likely.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: A flood forecast for the hills near a haor gives the rain for the next five days as 5 mm, 10 mm, 60 mm, 120 mm and 80 mm (example values). What is the best advice for the farmers?
options: Wait until day 5, then harvest everything.
Harvest only on day 4, when the rice is driest.
Do nothing, because the rain amounts are small.
Harvest on days 1 and 2, before the heavy rain starts.
questions.explanation: The heavy rain begins on day 3 and a flash flood could come soon after. Harvesting early saves most of the crop.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: Explain how wind is made. Use the words warm, rises and cool.
questions.model_answer: The Sun warms the ground, which warms the air above it. Warm air rises and cooler air moves in to take its place. This moving air is wind.
questions.explanation: Wind is air moving from a cooler place to take the place of warm air that has risen.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.stem: A class measured the temperature at 9 o'clock every morning for a week. Why did they measure at the same time each day?
questions.model_answer: So the results can be compared fairly, because the temperature changes during the day.
questions.explanation: The temperature rises and falls through the day, so measuring at different times would make the results unfair to compare.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a cyclone forms.
sequence: The Sun heats the sea above 27 °C.
Water evaporates and warm, damp air rises.
Huge clouds form as the vapour condenses.
Air rushes in to take its place and starts to spin.
The storm grows into a cyclone.
questions.explanation: Warm sea water evaporates, the warm damp air rises and cools, and clouds form. More air rushes in and spins because the Earth is spinning.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: A cyclone forms over warm sea water, warmer than about ___ °C.
questions.explanation: When the sea is warmer than about 27 °C, lots of water evaporates and feeds the storm.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: The same kind of storm has different names. Match each name to where it happens.
pairs: Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean
questions.explanation: A cyclone, a hurricane and a typhoon are the same kind of huge spinning storm. Only the name changes with the ocean.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Sort these wind speeds into the right kind of storm. (Depression: up to 61 km/h. Cyclonic storm: 62 to 88 km/h. Severe cyclonic storm: 89 to 117 km/h. Very severe cyclone: 118 km/h or more.)
questions.explanation: The stronger the winds, the stronger the storm: depression, cyclonic storm, severe cyclonic storm and very severe cyclone.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Which of these are dangers of a cyclone? Choose all that are right.
options: strong winds that blow down houses and trees
heavy rain that causes floods and landslides
a storm surge that floods villages and makes the soil salty
the sea becoming much colder
the soil becoming drier and drier
questions.explanation: A cyclone brings strong winds, heavy rain and a storm surge. They destroy homes and crops and flood the land with salty water.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Match each danger to what it does.
pairs: pushes salty sea water onto the land
questions.explanation: A storm surge is a wall of sea water pushed onto the land by the wind. It floods villages and makes the soil salty.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: A cyclone shelter is built on tall pillars so that it stands above the storm surge.
questions.explanation: The pillars lift the shelter above the flood water, so people inside stay safe.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Why do cyclones get weaker after they move over land?
options: Trees on land push the whole cyclone back out to sea.
The Earth spins more slowly when they are over land.
They lose the warm sea water that feeds them.
Land is always much colder than the sea at night.
questions.explanation: A cyclone gets its energy from warm sea water. Over land there is no warm water to feed it, so it loses energy.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Which warning signals mean great danger and tell people on the coast to go to a shelter?
options: 3, 4 and 5
5, 6 and 7
questions.explanation: Bangladesh warning signals go from 1 to 11 for the sea ports. The higher the number, the greater the danger. Signals 8, 9 and 10 mean great danger.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Burning coal, oil and gas adds more ___ to the air, and this traps heat.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide acts like a blanket and traps heat, so the Earth is slowly getting warmer.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how human actions can make cyclones more dangerous.
sequence: People burn coal, oil and gas.
More carbon dioxide is in the air.
Heat is trapped and the Earth warms.
The sea gets warmer.
Cyclones can become stronger.
questions.explanation: Burning fuels adds carbon dioxide, which traps heat. A warmer Earth means warmer seas, and warm seas can make cyclones stronger and wetter.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Why do most cyclones in the Bay of Bengal happen in April–May and October–November, and not in January?
questions.model_answer: The sea is warmest before and after the monsoon. In January the sea is cooler, so there is not enough warm, damp air to feed a cyclone.
questions.explanation: Cyclones need very warm sea water. In January the sea is cooler, so cyclones are rare.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Bangladesh produces only a tiny share of the world's carbon dioxide, but it is one of the countries most at risk from climate change.
questions.explanation: Much of Bangladesh is low and close to the sea, so rising sea level and stronger cyclones are serious dangers.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Look at the cyclone from above. Which number shows the **eye** of the cyclone?
questions.image_alt: A tropical cyclone seen from above with parts numbered.
questions.explanation: The eye (1) is the calm, clear centre of the cyclone. The strongest winds and rain are in the eye wall (2) around it.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Which number shows where the strongest winds and heaviest rain are found?
questions.image_alt: A tropical cyclone seen from above with parts numbered.
questions.explanation: The eye wall (2) is the ring of tall clouds around the eye. It has the strongest winds and rain. Rain bands (3) are further out.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Which picture shows a storm that forms over warm sea water?
questions.explanation: Cyclones form over warm seas. Snow, deserts and icebergs belong to cold or dry places.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Rahima's family is going to the cyclone shelter. Sort these pictures into things to take and things to leave at home.
questions.explanation: Take things you need to stay safe and healthy: drinking water, medicines and a torch. Heavy furniture, a television and a bed are too bulky to carry.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: In the picture, the winds of the cyclone spin round the eye in an anticlockwise direction.
questions.image_alt: A tropical cyclone seen from above with parts numbered.
questions.explanation: Cyclones north of the Equator spin anticlockwise because of the Earth's spin.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Rahima hears on the radio that the warning signal has gone up to 9. What should her family do?
options: Wait to see if the wind gets stronger.
Go to the river to see the waves.
Stay at home and cook dinner.
Go to the cyclone shelter now.
questions.explanation: Signal 9 means great danger. The family must go to the shelter straight away, before the winds and the storm surge arrive.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Rahima's family has goats and chickens. How can they keep the animals safe?
options: Tie them tightly to a tree in the open field.
Take them to raised ground near the shelter.
Leave them tied up in the field overnight.
Lock them inside the house until it is over.
questions.explanation: Animals can drown in a storm surge. Raised ground near the shelter (many shelters have space for animals) is much safer.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Rahima's grandmother cannot walk far. What is the best plan?
options: Let her walk to the shelter on her own.
Leave her at home with plenty of food and water.
Wait until the storm starts, then decide what to do.
Leave early and ask neighbours to help carry her.
questions.explanation: Older people, babies and people who are ill need extra help. Leaving early gives time to reach the shelter safely.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Volunteers help to spread cyclone warnings using megaphones, flags and mobile phone messages.
questions.explanation: Volunteers from the Cyclone Preparedness Programme walk through villages so that everyone, even people without a radio, hears the warning.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Which things should be on a family's "cyclone ready" checklist? Choose all that are right.
options: listen to the radio for the warning signal
know the way to the cyclone shelter
pack water, food, medicine and a torch
help neighbours who need it
stay outside to watch the storm come
questions.explanation: A good plan means listening to warnings, knowing the way, packing what you need and helping others. Staying outside is dangerous.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the temperature when you add more greenhouse gases?

sim.task: Open Greenhouse Effect. Find the control for the amount of greenhouse gases and the thermometer that shows the temperature. Start with a small amount of gases, then increase them and watch the temperature for a minute.

options: It goes up.
It goes down.
It stays the same.
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases trap heat. The more of them there are, the more heat is trapped and the hotter the Earth gets.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: In the simulation, what do greenhouse gases do to the heat that travels up from the ground?

sim.task: Open Greenhouse Effect. Add some greenhouse gases and watch what happens to the heat (infrared) waves that travel up from the ground when they reach the gases.

options: They let all of it escape straight into space.
They change the heat into sunlight again.
They trap some of it and send some back.
They make the heat disappear completely.
questions.explanation: Heat leaving the ground is absorbed by greenhouse gases, and some is sent back towards the surface. This is how the gases act like a blanket.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: In the simulation, the Earth is cooler with very few greenhouse gases than with many greenhouse gases.

sim.task: Open Greenhouse Effect. Set the greenhouse gases to a very small amount and note the temperature. Then set them to a large amount and compare.

questions.explanation: With fewer gases, less heat is trapped and more escapes into space, so the temperature is lower.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: The centre of Cyclone Sidr was at 15 °N on 13 November, 17.5 °N on 14 November and 21 °N on 15 November (rounded values). About how far north did it move each day on average between 13 and 15 November?
options: 1.5 degrees of latitude
7.5 degrees of latitude
6 degrees of latitude
3 degrees of latitude
questions.explanation: 21 − 15 = 6 degrees in 2 days, and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 degrees a day. Tracking the position each day helps scientists predict when a cyclone will reach land.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Example sea temperatures in the Bay of Bengal: 25 °C in January and 30 °C in May. In which month is a cyclone more likely, and why?
options: January, because the sea is cooler.
May, because the sea is warmer than 27 °C.
May, because the sea is colder than 27 °C.
January, because the sea is warmer than 27 °C.
questions.explanation: Cyclones need sea water warmer than about 27 °C. May's 30 °C is above that and January's 25 °C is below it.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Bangladesh is planting mangrove forests along the coast. Explain how this can protect people from cyclones and how it helps the climate.
questions.model_answer: Mangroves slow down the wind and the storm surge, so less water and wind reach villages. Trees also take in carbon dioxide, which helps slow climate change.
questions.explanation: Mangroves act like a green wall against wind and waves, and all trees take in carbon dioxide as they grow.

questions.title: Storms, Cyclones and Climate Change
questions.stem: Bangladesh produces only a tiny share of the world's carbon dioxide, so climate change cannot hurt Bangladesh.
questions.explanation: Climate change is global. Bangladesh is low and close to the sea, so it is one of the countries most at risk even though it adds little carbon dioxide.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: dropping mud and sand in a new place
soil and rocks sliding down a hill
questions.explanation: Weathering breaks rocks up, erosion carries the pieces away, and deposition drops them somewhere new.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Sort these into water erosion and wind erosion.
items: sand dunes moving on a beach
rain washing soil off a hill
questions.explanation: Moving water and moving air can both carry soil and sand away. Wind erosion is strongest where the land is dry and bare.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: When moving water or wind carries away soil and rock, this is called ___.
questions.explanation: Erosion carries pieces of rock and soil away. Weathering breaks the rock first, and deposition drops the pieces in a new place.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Rivers only take land away; they never build new land.
questions.explanation: Rivers drop mud and sand where the water slows down. Most of Bangladesh was built from mud carried by the Padma, Jamuna and Meghna rivers.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: What is a char?
options: a sand island that forms in a river
a tree that grows on a river bank
a long wall that holds back the sea
a boat that carries mud
questions.explanation: A char is a sand island that appears in the middle of a river where sand and mud are dropped.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Where does a river flow fastest and wear away its bank on a bend?
options: on the inside of the bend
on the outside of the bend
where the river meets the sea
in the shallow middle of the bend
questions.explanation: On the outside of a bend the water flows fastest and wears the bank away. On the inside the water slows down and drops mud.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a river builds new land.
sequence: Rain falls on the hills and flows into streams.
Fast-flowing water carries mud and sand down the river.
The river slows down near the sea.
The river drops the mud and sand and new land builds up.
questions.explanation: Fast water carries sediment. When the water slows down it can no longer carry it, so it drops the mud and sand.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Which of these help to slow down erosion? Choose all that are right.
options: planting trees and grass
cutting steps (terraces) into a hillside
placing geo-bags along a river bank
cutting down all the trees on a hillside
leaving soil bare and dry
questions.explanation: Roots hold soil, terraces slow the water running down a hill, and geo-bags protect a river bank. Cutting trees and leaving soil bare make erosion worse.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Match each way of slowing erosion to how it works.
pairs: roots hold the soil in place
a raised wall keeps river or sea water back
bags of sand placed along a river bank
steps cut into a hill slow the water running down
a row of trees slows the wind near the ground
questions.explanation: Each solution works in a different way and has good points and problems.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Which way of slowing erosion is quick to put in place along a river bank but can be washed away?
options: terraces
windbreaks
geo-bags
a planted forest
questions.explanation: Geo-bags are quick to place but a strong river can wash them away. Trees and terraces take longer to make.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: A system is a group of ___ that work together to do a job that no single part can do alone.
questions.explanation: A river is a system: rain, streams, the main river, its banks and the sea all work together to move water and mud.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Why is a coastal defence made of mangroves, an embankment and sluice gates called a system?
options: All the parts are made of exactly the same material.
It is very big and it is also very old.
Only one person builds all the different parts.
The parts work together to do a job.
questions.explanation: The mangroves slow the waves, the embankment holds back the water, and the gates let rain water out but keep the sea out. If one part fails, the whole system is weaker.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: If one part of a system stops working, the whole system is weaker.
questions.explanation: The parts of a system depend on each other. If the sluice gates fail, for example, the embankment cannot keep the sea out.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Why is erosion worse on a hill where all the trees have been cut down?
questions.model_answer: With no roots to hold the soil and no leaves to slow the rain, the rain washes the soil straight down the hill, causing erosion and landslides.
questions.explanation: Tree roots hold the soil and leaves slow the falling rain. Without them the rain washes the bare soil away.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: A row of trees or a fence that slows the wind is called a ___.
questions.explanation: A windbreak slows the wind near the ground, so less sand and soil is blown away. It protects fields and homes.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Where does the picture show new land forming where the river meets the sea?
questions.image_alt: A river from hills to the sea with processes numbered.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is deposition: the river slows down and drops mud and sand, building a delta. Number 2 is erosion and number 1 is weathering.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Look at the river picture. Match each number to what is happening.
questions.image_alt: A river from hills to the sea with processes numbered.
pairs: erosion: the river carries rock and soil
questions.explanation: Weathering breaks the rock, erosion carries the pieces away and deposition drops them in a new place.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Sort these pictures into things that can wear away land and things that help to protect it.
questions.explanation: Moving water and wind wear land away. Trees and plants protect it with their roots and leaves.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Wind builds sand dunes along the coast, like at Cox's Bazar. Which picture shows a place where you might find sand dunes?
questions.explanation: Wind blows dry sand into hills called dunes, along beaches. Mountains, cities and gardens do not have blowing sand dunes.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: In the river picture, the river deposits (drops) mud and sand where its water slows down near the sea.
questions.image_alt: A river from hills to the sea with processes numbered.
questions.explanation: Slow water cannot carry much. It drops its mud and sand, which builds up new land such as a delta.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Imran pours water on a pile of bare soil and on a pile of soil covered with grass. Which pile washes away faster, and why?
options: The grass-covered soil, because the grass is heavy.
Both piles wash away at exactly the same speed.
The bare soil, because grass protects the soil.
Neither pile washes away at all, even after a lot of rain.
questions.explanation: Plants protect soil. The roots hold it and the leaves slow the water. This is why hillsides with no plants suffer landslides.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Farmers want to grow crops on a steep hillside without the soil washing away. What could they build?
options: a straight, very steep slope with no steps
a deep pond at the top of the hill
a windbreak of tall trees along the hill
terraces: steps cut into the hillside
questions.explanation: Terraces slow the water running down a hill, so less soil is washed away. They are good for farming on hills but hard work to build.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Joy's family has a farm near a beach. Sand blows onto the fields. Which would help? Choose all that are right.
options: a row of trees as a windbreak
a fence along the edge of the field
keeping the soil covered or damp
leaving the field bare and dry
cutting down the trees around the field
questions.explanation: Windbreaks, fences and damp or covered soil slow the wind or keep the sand in place. Bare, dry soil and no trees would make it worse.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: A storm surge is coming. What would happen if the sluice gates in an embankment were left open?
options: Rain water could never drain away.
Sea water would flow into the fields behind the embankment.
The embankment would grow taller.
The mangroves would stop all the water.
questions.explanation: Sluice gates let rain water out but must be closed to keep the sea out. If they are left open, sea water floods the fields and makes the soil salty.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: A new char can be washed away by floods.
questions.explanation: Chars are made of loose sand and mud. A family on a new char gets new land, but a flood can take it away again.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Class 4B put 200 g of dry sand in each tray and blew air over it for 1 minute. Sand lost: tray A (nothing) 90 g, tray B (windbreak) 30 g, tray C (windbreak and damp sand) 5 g. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The windbreak made no difference to the sand lost.
A windbreak cut the sand lost by 60 g, and damp sand lost even less.
Damp sand lost more sand than dry sand.
Tray A kept the most sand.
questions.explanation: 90 − 30 = 60 g less sand was lost with the windbreak. Tray C lost only 5 g, so damp sand with a windbreak lost the least.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: The land lost to the river at one village in five years (example data) was 12, 30, 8, 22 and 10 hectares. What was the total land lost?
options: 82 hectares
72 hectares
92 hectares
102 hectares
questions.explanation: 12 + 30 + 8 + 22 + 10 = 82 hectares. The two worst years (30 and 22) were the years with very big monsoon floods.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Why might protecting one part of a river bank make erosion worse further along the river?
questions.model_answer: The water cannot wear away the protected bank, so it is pushed with more force against the next unprotected bank and erodes it faster.
questions.explanation: The river still has the same energy. If one place is protected, the water may attack another place harder.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: A fast river is eating away a village bank. Geo-bags are quick and cheaper but can be washed away. Trees are cheap and natural but too slow to help now. Which plan is best?
options: Only plant trees and wait years for them to grow.
Do nothing, because the river will always win.
Only use geo-bags and never plant anything else.
Geo-bags now, then grass and trees behind them.
questions.explanation: The best plan uses the strengths of both: geo-bags work quickly, and the roots of trees and grass give long-term protection.

questions.title: Changing Landscapes
questions.stem: Class 4B tests two trays. Tray A has no windbreak and a fan blows for 1 minute. Tray B has a windbreak and the fan blows for 2 minutes. Why is this not a fair test?
options: Both trays have the same amount of dry sand in them.
A fan was used instead of real wind outdoors.
The fan time is different as well as the windbreak.
Tray B has more than one stick in the windbreak.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing changes (the windbreak). The fan time, speed, distance and amount of sand must stay the same.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Sort these resources into renewable and finite.
questions.explanation: Sunlight, wind, trees and fish are replaced naturally if we use them carefully. Oil, coal, gas and metals took millions of years to form and will run out.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Match each action to the resource it saves.
questions.explanation: Each action helps a resource last longer. Conserving means using resources carefully so that they do not run out.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Water ___ round and round in the water cycle, but coal and gas will one day ___.
questions.explanation: Water is used and returns to the environment to be used again. Coal and gas are finite: once they are used up, they are gone.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Natural gas is a renewable resource.
questions.explanation: Natural gas took millions of years to form and cannot be replaced, so it is finite. When it is used up, it is gone.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: What does it mean to **conserve** a resource?
options: use it as fast as possible
throw it away when finished
use it carefully so it lasts
sell it all to other countries
questions.explanation: To conserve means to use something carefully so that it lasts for a long time.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which of these are renewable if we use them carefully? Choose all that are right.
options: sunlight
wind
coal
trees
natural gas
questions.explanation: Sunlight, wind and trees are replaced naturally. Coal and natural gas are finite. Trees are renewable only if we plant new ones and do not cut them faster than they grow.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Most of Bangladesh's electricity has been made by burning natural gas. Why is this a worry for the future?
options: Gas can only be used in the winter.
The gas fields are slowly running out.
Gas makes the electricity too cold.
There are far too many gas fields.
questions.explanation: Natural gas is finite. As the fields run out, the country is building more solar power and buying fuel from abroad.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Put the steps of the water cycle in order.
sequence: Water evaporates from rivers and seas.
The water vapour cools and condenses into clouds.
Rain falls from the clouds.
The water flows back to the sea.
questions.explanation: Water goes round and round: it evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain, and flows back to the rivers and sea.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which is a problem with some tube-wells in Bangladesh?
options: Some of the water contains arsenic, a poison.
The water is always too hot to drink.
They use up the coal under the ground.
They only work in the dry season.
questions.explanation: Tube-wells give safe water instead of dirty ponds, but some wells have arsenic. Too much pumping can also lower the water underground.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Solar panels cause no problems at all.
questions.explanation: Solar panels give clean electricity, but old panels and batteries must be recycled safely so they do not pollute.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: In social forestry, communities plant and care for ___.
questions.explanation: Planting and protecting forests helps to conserve wood, soil and wildlife.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Why is it a problem if people catch fish faster than the fish can breed?
questions.model_answer: There will be fewer and fewer fish until they run out, so there is no food or work later.
questions.explanation: A renewable resource only stays renewable if it is not used faster than it is replaced. That is why there is a ban on catching hilsa while they lay eggs.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which of these is a **sudden** change to a resource?
options: the water underground getting lower each year
a forest slowly growing taller
fish numbers slowly falling each year
a cyclone knocks down a forest in one day
questions.explanation: A cyclone can destroy a forest in a day. Changes that take years, like falling groundwater, are gradual.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Sort these changes into sudden and gradual.
items: a flash flood washes away a crop
fish numbers fall slowly over many years
the soil slowly becomes more salty
questions.explanation: Sudden changes happen in a day or less. Gradual changes happen slowly and are harder to notice, but they are just as important.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Scientists measure resources every year because slow changes are hard to notice but just as important as sudden ones.
questions.explanation: Measuring every year shows gradual changes, such as groundwater falling, before it is too late to act.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which number shows **evaporation** in the water cycle?
questions.image_alt: The water cycle with stages numbered.
questions.explanation: In evaporation (1) the Sun heats water in seas and rivers and it turns into vapour. Condensation (2) forms clouds and rain (3) falls from them.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Look at the water cycle. Match each number to what happens.
questions.image_alt: The water cycle with stages numbered.
pairs: water collects in rivers and seas
questions.explanation: The numbers show evaporation, condensation, precipitation (rain) and collection.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which picture shows a way to make electricity from a renewable resource?
questions.explanation: Solar panels make electricity from sunlight, which is renewable. The others come from burning or spilling fuels, which are finite.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which pictures show resources that are renewable if we use them carefully? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Sunlight, wind and fish are replaced naturally. A gem stone is a mineral that took a very long time to form and cannot be replaced.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: In the picture, water vapour cools and forms clouds at number 2.
questions.image_alt: The water cycle with stages numbered.
questions.explanation: Number 2 is condensation: water vapour cools and turns back into tiny drops of water that make clouds.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Sumi notices that a tap in the school yard drips all day. What should she do?
options: Leave it, because water never runs out.
Open it fully to wash the drain.
Tell a teacher so it can be fixed.
Ignore it, because it is only a drop.
questions.explanation: A dripping tap wastes a lot of water over a day. Reporting leaks helps to save water.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: A test kit shows that the water from a family's tube-well has arsenic in it. What should they do?
options: Use a safe well or tested water instead.
Drink it because it is cold and clear.
Keep drinking it for just one more week.
Wait for the arsenic to sink to the bottom of the jug.
questions.explanation: Arsenic is a poison and cannot be seen or tasted. Scientists made test kits so families can find safe wells.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: On the south-west coast, pond and underground water have become salty. Why is rainwater stored in a clean tank a good choice for drinking?
options: Rainwater has extra salt from the sea.
Rain is fresh water and is not salty.
Rainwater only falls in the dry season.
Rainwater is always very cold.
questions.explanation: Rain is fresh water. The monsoon brings plenty, so a family can store it for the dry season. Rain is also a renewable resource.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which actions save water at home? Choose all that are right.
options: turning taps off tightly
fixing leaks
collecting rainwater
leaving the tap running while brushing teeth
washing the floor with fresh drinking water every day
questions.explanation: Turning off taps, fixing leaks and collecting rainwater save water. Leaving the tap running and washing floors with drinking water waste it.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Nadia's family cooks on a stove that uses a lot of wood and makes a lot of smoke. What would help most?
options: a bigger fire
burning plastic as well
a cleaner cookstove that uses less wood
cooking all day long
questions.explanation: Scientists have designed cleaner cookstoves that use less wood and make less smoke. This saves trees and is better for health.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: A dripping tap wastes 50 ml of water in 10 minutes. How much water does it waste in one day (24 hours)?
options: 1.2 litres
7.2 litres
12 litres
72 litres
questions.explanation: In one hour there are six 10-minute periods: 6 × 50 = 300 ml. In 24 hours: 24 × 300 = 7200 ml = 7.2 litres.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: 1 mm of rain falling on 1 square metre of roof gives 1 litre of water. A school roof has an area of 40 square metres. In one storm 50 mm of rain falls. How much water can be collected?
options: 90 litres
200 litres
2000 litres
20 000 litres
questions.explanation: 40 × 50 = 2000 litres. Rainwater harvesting can store this for the dry season.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: "Trees are renewable, so we can cut down as many as we like." Do you agree? Explain.
questions.model_answer: No. Trees are only renewable if we plant new ones and let them grow. If we cut them faster than they grow, forests disappear.
questions.explanation: A resource is renewable only if it is replaced as fast as we use it.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which statements about technology are fair? Choose all that are right.
options: Tube-wells gave many people safe water, but some wells have arsenic.
Plastic is cheap and light, but it lasts hundreds of years as litter.
Solar panels give clean electricity, but old panels must be recycled safely.
Motor boats and cars burn no fuel.
Technology never has any problems.
questions.explanation: Technology can both help and harm. Tube-wells, plastic and solar panels each have good points and problems.

questions.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: A pond has 100 fish. Each year 30 new fish are born (example). What is the most the villagers can catch each year if the number of fish is not to go down?
options: 30 fish
15 fish
60 fish
100 fish
questions.explanation: If they catch only as many as are born (30), the pond stays at 100 fish. Catching more means the number of fish falls every year, which is not sustainable.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Matter is anything that…
options: can be seen and touched
has mass and takes up space
is hot or cold
is always a solid
questions.explanation: Matter has mass and takes up space. This includes things we cannot see, such as air.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Air is matter, even though we cannot see it.
questions.explanation: Air takes up space and has mass. When you blow up a balloon, you can see the air taking up space.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.subskill: Particles in solids, liquids and gases
questions.stem: In a ___, the particles are packed tightly in rows and can only vibrate.
questions.explanation: Solid particles cannot move around. They only vibrate in their places, which is why a solid keeps its shape.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.subskill: Particles in solids, liquids and gases
questions.stem: Match each state of matter to what its particles are like.
pairs: packed tightly in rows; they only vibrate
close together but able to slide past each other
far apart and moving fast in all directions
questions.explanation: The way the particles are arranged gives each state its properties: a solid keeps its shape, a liquid flows, and a gas spreads out.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Sort these into solid, liquid or gas.
questions.explanation: A solid keeps its shape, a liquid flows and fills the bottom of its container, and a gas spreads out to fill all the space it can.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Match each everyday event to the change of state.
pairs: wet clothes drying in the sun
candle wax dripping near the flame
water turning into ice in a freezer
steam turning into drops on a pot lid
questions.explanation: Melting: solid to liquid. Freezing: liquid to solid. Evaporating: liquid to gas. Condensing: gas to liquid.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show what happens when an ice cube is heated for a long time.
sequence: A solid ice cube is heated.
The ice melts into liquid water.
The water gets hotter until it reaches 100 °C.
The water boils and turns into steam, a gas.
questions.explanation: Heating a solid makes it melt into a liquid. Heating the liquid more makes it boil at its boiling point and become a gas.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Pure water freezes at ___ °C and boils at ___ °C.
questions.explanation: Pure water melts and freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: A kitchen is 36 °C. Melting points: butter 32 °C, chocolate 34 °C, candle wax 60 °C, iron 1538 °C, ice 0 °C. Which of these would melt if left in the kitchen? Choose all that are right.
options: butter
chocolate
candle wax
an iron spoon
ice
questions.explanation: A solid melts when the temperature is above its melting point. 36 °C is above 32 °C, 34 °C and 0 °C, but below 60 °C and 1538 °C.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Which of these is a pure substance?
options: sea water
soil
air
sugar
questions.explanation: A pure substance contains only one kind of material. Sea water (water and salt), soil and air (many gases) are all mixtures.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Match each substance to what it is made of.
pairs: hydrogen and oxygen atoms joined together
sodium and chlorine atoms joined together
water and salt mixed but not joined
questions.explanation: An element has one kind of atom. A compound has two or more kinds of atom joined together. A mixture is not joined: the substances are just mixed.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Sort these into element, compound or mixture.
questions.explanation: Oxygen, iron and copper have only one kind of atom. Water, carbon dioxide and salt have joined atoms of different kinds. Air, soil and cha are different substances mixed together.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Nadia says: 'Salt is an element because it is pure.' Is she right?
questions.explanation: Salt is pure, but it is a compound. It is made of two kinds of atom, sodium and chlorine, joined together. An element has only one kind of atom.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.subskill: Particles in solids, liquids and gases
questions.stem: Use the particle model to explain why a liquid takes the shape of its container.
questions.model_answer: The particles in a liquid are close together but can slide past each other, so the liquid flows to fill the bottom of the container.
questions.explanation: Liquid particles are not locked in rows like a solid, so they can move past one another. The liquid keeps its volume but spreads out to fit the container.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.subskill: Particles in solids, liquids and gases
questions.stem: Look at the gas box. What do the small arrows on the particles show?
questions.image_alt: Three boxes of particles: solid packed in rows, liquid touching but jumbled, and gas far apart with small arrows. Arrows between the boxes are labelled melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing.
options: They move fast in all directions.
They are pulled downwards.
They sit in neat rows.
They are getting colder.
questions.explanation: Gas particles are far apart and move fast in all directions. That is why a gas spreads out to fill any space.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Steam touches a cold pot lid and turns into drops of water. Find this change in the picture. What is it called?
questions.image_alt: Three boxes of particles: solid packed in rows, liquid touching but jumbled, and gas far apart. Arrows between the boxes are labelled melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing.
options: Freezing: liquid to solid
Evaporating: liquid to gas
Condensing: gas to liquid
Melting: solid to liquid
questions.explanation: Steam is a gas. When it cools on the lid it becomes liquid water, so the change is condensing, shown by the arrow from gas back to liquid.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Look at the particles in the picture. Why can you squash a gas, but not a solid?
questions.image_alt: Three boxes of particles: solid packed in rows, liquid touching but jumbled, and gas with only a few particles far apart.
options: Solid particles move faster than gas particles.
Gas particles are smaller than solid particles.
Gas particles are packed in rows.
Gas particles are far apart, so they can be pushed closer together.
questions.explanation: In a gas there is a lot of empty space between the particles, so they can be pushed closer. Solid particles are already touching.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Look at the pictures. Sort them into solid or liquid.
questions.explanation: Ice, rock and wood keep their shape. Milk, water and honey flow and take the shape of their container.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Butter melts at 32 °C and chocolate melts at 34 °C. Three thermometers show the temperature in three different places. In which place will both butter and chocolate melt?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C showing 5 °C, 25 °C and 40 °C.
options: A
B
C
questions.explanation: Thermometer C shows 40 °C, which is above both 32 °C and 34 °C. A (5 °C) and B (25 °C) are below both melting points.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Priya wants to carry a bar of chocolate to school on a 36 °C day in Dhaka. Chocolate melts at 34 °C. What is the best way to keep it solid?
options: Put it in a black bag in the sun.
Pack it with a cold ice pack in a lunch box.
Leave it on top of her bag.
Keep it in her warm pocket.
questions.explanation: The day is hotter than chocolate's melting point, so chocolate will melt unless it is kept cool. An ice pack keeps the temperature below 34 °C.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: A health worker in a village in Sylhet is teaching families about mixtures at home. Which of these are mixtures? Choose all that are right.
options: the air we breathe
ORS drink (salt, sugar and water)
pure sugar
sea water
pure oxygen gas
questions.explanation: A mixture has two or more substances mixed together. Air, ORS drink and sea water are mixtures. Pure sugar and pure oxygen each contain only one substance.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.subskill: Uses of mixtures and pure substances
questions.stem: Imran's mother stirs oral rehydration salt (ORS) powder into a jug of clean water for his sister, who has diarrhoea. Imran says: 'The drink is a mixture.' Is he right?
questions.explanation: ORS is a carefully measured mixture of salt, sugar and water. It was developed and tested in Bangladesh and India, including at icddr,b in Dhaka, and has saved millions of children's lives.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.subskill: Uses of mixtures and pure substances
questions.stem: A goldsmith in Dhaka mixes a little copper into the gold before making a ring. Why?
options: It makes the ring a pure substance.
Copper turns the gold into a compound.
The mixture is harder, so the ring keeps its shape.
Copper makes the gold melt at 0 °C.
questions.explanation: Gold jewellery is usually a mixture of gold with a little copper. The mixture is harder than soft pure gold. Mixing does not join the atoms, so it is not a compound.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Fishers in Cox's Bazar pack hilsa in crushed ice, not in one big block. Why is crushed ice better?
options: Small pieces fit closely around every fish and touch more of its surface.
Crushed ice is colder than a big block of ice.
Crushed ice does not melt.
A big block is made from a different material.
questions.explanation: Crushed ice and a big block are both at 0 °C and both melt. Small pieces touch more of each fish, so the fish cool faster and stay fresh.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.subskill: Particles in solids, liquids and gases
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the particles as you go from solid to liquid to gas?

sim.task: Open States of Matter and stay on the States screen. Choose Water. Press Solid, then Liquid, then Gas. Watch how close together the particles are and how fast they move each time.

options: They stay the same distance apart but change colour.
They get closer together and move slower each time.
They get further apart and move faster each time.
They disappear and then come back.
questions.explanation: Solid particles are packed in rows and only vibrate. Liquid particles are close but slide around. Gas particles are far apart and move fastest.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: In the simulation, when you add heat to the solid, its particles move faster and the thermometer reading goes up.

sim.task: Open States of Matter and stay on the States screen. Choose Water and press Solid. Use the heat/cool control to add heat slowly. Watch the particles and the thermometer.

questions.explanation: Heating gives the particles more energy, so they move faster and the temperature rises. If you keep heating, the solid melts into a liquid and then becomes a gas.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Rumi plans a melting race. She puts a big block of ice in the shade, a small cube of butter in the sun and a medium piece of chocolate on a plate indoors. How can she make it a fair test of how fast different solids melt?
options: Use a bigger piece of butter and chocolate.
Use the same size cube of each solid, on the same type of lid, in the same sunny place.
Time each one with a different clock.
Put the ice in the shade and the others in the sun.
questions.explanation: In a fair test we change only the type of solid and keep everything else the same: size, lid, place and start time. Then any difference in melting time comes from the solid.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Example results: crushed ice is warmed gently with a thermometer in it. Readings: 0 min −4 °C, 2 min 0 °C, 4 min 0 °C, 6 min 0 °C, 8 min 3 °C. Ice was still floating at 6 min. Why did the reading stay at 0 °C from 2 to 6 minutes?
options: The ice was melting, so the temperature stayed at 0 °C until all the ice had melted.
The heater stopped working.
The thermometer was broken.
The water was boiling.
questions.explanation: While ice is melting, its temperature stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted. After that, at 8 min, the liquid water warms up.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: On a hot day, drops of water appear on the outside of a cold bottle taken from the fridge. The bottle is not leaking. Explain where the drops come from.
questions.model_answer: Water vapour (a gas) in the warm air touches the cold bottle, cools down and condenses into liquid water drops.
questions.explanation: Air always contains some water vapour. When it touches the cold bottle it cools and changes state from gas to liquid, which is condensing.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.subskill: Using ice to keep food fresh
questions.stem: Example numbers: a fishing boat needs 2 kg of ice for every 1 kg of fish. It has 600 kg of ice on board and catches 350 kg of fish. How much more ice does it need?
options: 700 kg
175 kg
100 kg
250 kg
questions.explanation: 350 kg of fish needs 350 × 2 = 700 kg of ice. The boat has 600 kg, so it needs 700 − 600 = 100 kg more. Keeping fish cold stops germs growing fast.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: What happens when you stir sugar into a glass of water?
options: The sugar floats on top.
The sugar sinks and stays as lumps.
The sugar dissolves and seems to disappear.
The sugar turns into oil.
questions.explanation: Sugar dissolves in water: it breaks up into tiny pieces that spread through the water, so we cannot see it any more.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Sort these by what happens when you put them in water and stir.
questions.explanation: Sugar and salt dissolve. Stones and sand do not dissolve and sink to the bottom. Oil does not mix with water and floats on top, like a dry stick.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Match each mixture to the best way to separate it.
questions.explanation: We choose a method that uses a different property of the things in the mixture: size, whether they are magnetic, how light they are, or whether they dissolve.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: When rice is tossed on a kula, the wind blows the husks away because they are lighter than the rice grains.
questions.explanation: This is called winnowing. The light husks are carried away by the wind, and the heavier rice grains fall back down.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: A filter separates bits of ___ from a ___.
questions.explanation: In filtering, the liquid passes through the filter paper or cloth and the solid bits stay behind.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: When salt dissolves in water, it is gone for ever and can never be got back.
questions.explanation: The salt is still there, in tiny pieces. If you leave the salty water in the sun, the water evaporates and the salt is left behind.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how scrap aluminium becomes a cooking pot in an Old Dhaka workshop.
sequence: A collector buys old aluminium from homes.
The scrap is heated until it melts.
The liquid metal is poured into a sand mould.
The metal cools and becomes solid.
The new pot is taken out of the mould.
questions.explanation: Heating melts the solid metal. When the liquid metal cools in the mould it freezes into the shape of the mould, so old metal becomes a new pot.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to get both the sand and the salt back from a mixture of sand and salt.
sequence: Stir the mixture into water; the salt dissolves.
Pour it through filter paper; the sand stays behind.
Collect the salty water that passes through.
Leave the salty water in the sun.
The water evaporates and the salt is left.
questions.explanation: The salt dissolves but the sand does not, so filtering takes out the sand. Evaporating the water then leaves the salt.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: When salt ___ in water, it breaks into tiny pieces that pass through filter paper.
questions.explanation: Dissolved pieces are far too small to be caught by a filter. That is why we use evaporating, not filtering, to get salt back.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Which of these mixtures could you separate using a magnet? Choose all that are right.
options: iron pins mixed with sand
sugar dissolved in water
iron nails mixed with rice
salt mixed with sand
plastic beads mixed with wooden beads
questions.explanation: A magnet pulls out iron. Sand, rice, salt, sugar, plastic and wood are not magnetic, so a magnet cannot separate them from each other.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Why can't you get salt out of salty water by pouring it through filter paper?
options: The salt has dissolved, so its tiny pieces go through with the water.
Salt melts when it touches the paper.
Salt is too heavy for the paper.
The paper soaks up all the water.
questions.explanation: Dissolved salt is in pieces far too small to be trapped by the paper. We evaporate the water to get the salt back.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: A mould for liquid metal must be made of something with a much higher melting point than the metal. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: If the mould had a lower melting point, the hot liquid metal would melt the mould.
questions.explanation: The mould must stay solid while the hot liquid metal is poured in, so its melting point must be much higher than the metal's.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: When vinegar and baking soda are mixed, the fizzing shows that a new gas is being made.
questions.explanation: Fizzing means a gas is made. This is different from salt dissolving, because the gas escapes and you cannot get the vinegar and baking soda back.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Mud is left to sink to the bottom of a bucket of water. Then Nadia carefully pours the clear water off the top. This method is called…
options: winnowing
evaporating
using a magnet
decanting (pouring off)
questions.explanation: Letting a solid sink and then pouring the liquid off the top is called decanting. Filtering would catch the smaller bits that are left.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Look at the picture of filtering muddy water. Which number shows the solid that is left behind in the filter paper?
questions.image_alt: Filtering muddy water with a funnel and filter paper over a beaker. Parts are numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is the solid left behind in the filter paper. Number 2 is the filter paper, 1 is the funnel and 4 is the clear water that passes through.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Look at the picture. Why does the clear water (4) pass through the paper, while the solid (3) stays behind?
questions.image_alt: Filtering muddy water with a funnel and filter paper over a beaker. Parts are numbered 1 to 5.
options: The solid is hotter than the water.
The holes in the paper are too small for the solid pieces but big enough for water.
The water is lighter, so it floats through the paper.
The beaker pulls the water down.
questions.explanation: Filter paper has tiny holes. Water passes through them but the bigger bits of solid are trapped. This is separating by size.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Match each picture to the separating job it can do.
pairs: pulls iron pins out of sand
evaporates the water from salty water
blows light husks away from rice
questions.explanation: Each helper uses a different property: a magnet attracts iron, the Sun's heat evaporates water, wind blows away light husks, and hands can pick out big pieces.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Look at the pictures. Which of these can be recycled by melting and moulding into new things? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Metals, glass and plastic can be melted, poured into a mould and cooled to make something new. Paper and fruit cannot be melted and moulded this way.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Which tool would be best for pulling iron pins out of a pile of sand?
questions.explanation: A magnet attracts iron but not sand, so it pulls the pins out and leaves the sand behind.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
