questions.stem: In an Old Dhaka workshop, liquid aluminium is poured into a sand mould and left to cool. What change of state happens as it cools?
options: solid to liquid
gas to liquid
liquid to gas
liquid to solid
questions.explanation: Cooling makes the liquid metal freeze into a solid in the shape of the mould.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: After threshing, Joy's grandfather has rice mixed with light husks. It is a breezy afternoon. What should he do?
options: Toss the rice on a kula so the wind blows the husks away.
Leave the rice in the sun until it evaporates.
Hold a magnet over the rice.
Pour the rice through filter paper.
questions.explanation: Winnowing uses wind to blow away the light husks. A magnet only works on iron, rice does not evaporate, and filter paper is for solids in liquids.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Raju filters muddy pond water through sand and cloth, and it now looks clear. What should he do before anyone drinks it?
options: Drink it, because clear water is always safe.
Boil it or treat it, because germs are too small to see.
Add some salt to it.
Put it in the freezer.
questions.explanation: Filtering can take out mud, but germs and dissolved poisons are far too small to see and can still pass through. Clear water must still be boiled or treated.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Water from a tubewell in a village contains dissolved arsenic, which you cannot see, smell or taste. Why can't ordinary cloth remove it?
options: The cloth is too thick.
The arsenic is dissolved, in pieces far too small for the cloth to trap.
Arsenic is a gas that escapes.
Arsenic floats on top of the water.
questions.explanation: Like salt in water, dissolved arsenic is in tiny pieces that pass through cloth. A special layer, such as the iron mixture in the SONO filter, is needed to grab it.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: The SONO filter was invented by Dr Abul Hussam to make tubewell water safer. Match each layer in the buckets to its job.
pairs: trap bits of mud and sand
questions.explanation: Each layer does a different job. The filter needs no electricity, so families can use it at home.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: The SONO filter needs no electricity, so families in villages without power can still use it.
questions.explanation: Water just trickles down through the layers in the buckets. A design that is simple, cheap and needs no electricity works well for villages.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Which method would you use to separate each mixture? Sort them.
items: salt from sea water in shallow pans
questions.explanation: Use the property that is different: iron is magnetic, mud and leaves are solid bits in a liquid, dissolved salt stays when water evaporates, and husks are lighter than grain.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Example results from Class 4C (clearness rating: 1 = very muddy, 5 = very clear): cotton cloth 2, sand 3, filter paper 4, sand + charcoal 5. Priya says: 'Sand + charcoal scored 5, so its water is safe to drink.' What is the best reply?
options: She is right, because 5 is the top score.
She is right if the water also smells fine.
Clear water can still hold germs and poisons, so it needs boiling or treating.
She is wrong, because charcoal makes water dirty.
questions.explanation: The rating only measures how clear the water looks. Germs and dissolved poisons like arsenic are too small to see, so clear-looking water may still be unsafe.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Why is melting an old aluminium pot to make a new one a reversible change, but burning paper is not?
options: Melting only changes the state: the liquid metal can freeze again. Burning makes new substances that cannot be changed back.
Metal is heavier than paper.
Paper cannot be heated.
Burning is slower than melting.
questions.explanation: Melting is a change of state, so the metal is still the same substance and can become solid again. Burning paper makes ash, smoke and gases, which cannot be turned back into paper.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Tuli spilled a mixture of rice grains, iron nails and salt. Describe how she could get all three back, in a sensible order.
questions.model_answer: Use a magnet to pull out the iron nails. Add water to dissolve the salt, then sieve or filter out the rice. Evaporate the water to get the salt back.
questions.explanation: Use each property in turn: the nails are magnetic, the salt dissolves and the rice does not, and evaporating leaves the salt behind. Salt must come last because it only separates when dissolved.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.stem: Example: sieve A has holes 4 mm wide and sieve B has holes 2 mm wide. A mixture has pieces that are 1 mm, 3 mm and 6 mm wide. It is poured through sieve A, and what passes through is poured through sieve B. Which pieces are left on sieve B?
options: the 6 mm pieces
the 1 mm pieces
the 1 mm and 3 mm pieces
the 3 mm pieces
questions.explanation: Sieve A holds back the 6 mm pieces. The 1 mm and 3 mm pieces pass through. Sieve B holds back the 3 mm pieces, and only the 1 mm pieces pass through both.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Air, water, a mango and a mobile phone are all made of tiny particles called…
options: germs
sand grains
atoms
sparks
questions.explanation: All matter is made of atoms. They are incredibly small: the full stop at the end of a sentence contains millions and millions of them.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: An electron is heavier than a proton.
questions.explanation: An electron is very light, about 2000 times lighter than a proton. Protons and neutrons are the heavy particles.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: The tiny centre of an atom is called the ___. Very light ___ move around it.
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons. The electrons move very fast in the space around it.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Match each particle to its electric charge.
questions.explanation: Protons are positive, electrons are negative, and neutrons have no charge.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Sort these facts by the particle they describe.
items: is about 2000 times lighter than a proton
questions.explanation: Each particle has its own charge and place in the atom. The number of protons decides which element an atom is, and the electron is by far the lightest particle.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Neutrons have no electric charge.
questions.explanation: Neutrons are neutral. They sit in the nucleus with the protons and add to the mass of the atom.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: What decides which element an atom is?
options: its number of protons
its size
its colour
its number of neutrons
questions.explanation: Every hydrogen atom has 1 proton, every carbon atom 6 and every oxygen atom 8. The number of protons decides the element.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Which two kinds of particle are found in the nucleus?
options: protons and electrons
neutrons and electrons
only electrons
protons and neutrons
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons. Electrons are outside it, moving around.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: An electron is lighter than a proton. How much lighter?
options: about 2 times lighter
about 2000 times lighter
about 20 times lighter
exactly the same mass
questions.explanation: An electron is about 2000 times lighter than a proton, which is why we leave electrons out when we add up the mass of an atom.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Put these discoveries about the atom in the order they happened.
sequence: Democritus names the atom (about 400 BCE).
Dalton says each element is made of its own atoms (1803).
Thomson discovers the electron (1897).
Rutherford discovers the nucleus (1911).
Chadwick discovers the neutron (1932).
questions.explanation: Each scientist used new evidence to improve the model of the atom. Our ideas about atoms changed many times over hundreds of years.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Which of these statements about atoms are right? Choose all that are right.
options: Atoms are mostly empty space.
An atom has the same number of protons and electrons.
Electrons are found in the nucleus.
There are about 118 kinds of atom.
Neutrons have a positive charge.
questions.explanation: An atom is mostly empty space, protons and electrons are equal in number, and there are about 118 kinds of atom, one for each element. Electrons are outside the nucleus and neutrons have no charge.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Most of the mass of an atom is in its nucleus. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons, which are heavy, while the electrons outside it are very light.
questions.explanation: Protons and neutrons each count as 1 unit of mass, but an electron is about 2000 times lighter, so nearly all the mass is in the nucleus.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Match each element to the number of protons in each of its atoms.
questions.explanation: The number of protons is different for every element. Hydrogen is the lightest, with just 1 proton.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: A molecule of water is made when two hydrogen atoms join with one oxygen atom.
questions.explanation: Atoms can join together to make molecules. Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: What is a molecule?
options: a very large atom
a particle with a negative charge
two or more atoms joined together
the centre of an atom
questions.explanation: A molecule is two or more atoms joined together, such as the two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom in water.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Which picture is often used as the symbol for an atom?
questions.explanation: The atom symbol shows a small centre with paths of electrons around it. It is a model, not an exact drawing of a real atom.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Look at the pictures. Which can you see with just your eyes, and which are too small to see? Sort them.
categories: Too small to see with your eyes
items: Too small to see with your eyes
Too small to see with your eyes
questions.explanation: Atoms are far too small to see, even smaller than microbes, which need a microscope. Yet everything we can see, such as an ant, a mango or an elephant, is made of atoms.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Each dot in this picture stands for a tiny particle of matter. What does the picture tell us about solids, liquids and gases?
questions.image_alt: Three boxes of particles: solid packed in rows, liquid touching but jumbled, and gas far apart. Arrows between the boxes are labelled melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing.
options: Only gases are made of particles.
Solids are not made of particles.
Liquids are made of one big particle.
They are all made of tiny particles, arranged in different ways.
questions.explanation: All matter is made of tiny particles such as atoms and molecules. What changes between a solid, a liquid and a gas is how the particles are arranged and how they move.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Iron is an element. Which of these is made mostly of iron?
questions.explanation: Iron is a hard metal used for things like nuts and bolts, pots and stoves. Wax, wood and ice are made of other substances.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: A model is a way of showing something that is too big, too small or too far away to see directly. Which picture shows a model?
questions.explanation: A globe is a small model of the whole Earth. Scientists also use drawings, balls and sticks, and computer pictures as models of atoms.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Priya makes a clay model of a carbon atom. A carbon atom has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and the right number of electrons. Which pieces does she need?
options: 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 12 electrons
12 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons
6 protons, 0 neutrons and 6 electrons
6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons
questions.explanation: An atom has the same number of electrons as protons, so the charges balance. Carbon has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Imran builds an atom model with a clay ball and beads on neat circles around it. He says, 'This is exactly what a real atom looks like.' What is the best reply?
options: Yes, scientists have photographed atoms like this.
It is a useful model, but real electrons do not move in neat circles and the nucleus is far smaller.
No, atoms are solid balls.
No, models are never useful.
questions.explanation: Models help us think about things we cannot see, but they are not exactly like the real thing. In a real atom the nucleus is tiny and electrons do not move in neat circles.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: A goldsmith in Dhaka tells Mina that every gold atom has 79 protons. So a gold atom has ___ electrons.
questions.explanation: An atom has the same number of electrons as protons, so the positive and negative charges balance and the atom has no overall charge.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Mr Rahman shows a marble in the middle of a football field to model an atom's nucleus. This model shows that most of an atom is empty space.
questions.explanation: If the nucleus were a marble in the middle of a football field, the electrons would be like tiny specks of dust flying around the edges of the stadium, with empty space between.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Nobody has ever seen inside an atom with their eyes. How do scientists know what atoms are like? Choose all that are right.
options: They do experiments and collect evidence.
They change their models when new evidence appears.
They look at atoms through a hand lens.
They use models such as drawings and computer pictures.
They guess without doing any tests.
questions.explanation: Scientists combine experiments with creative thinking. When new evidence did not fit the old model, such as the electron, nucleus and neutron discoveries, they changed the model.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Example: an atom X has 5 protons and 6 neutrons. Remember: mass = protons + neutrons. Its mass is ___ units and it has ___ electrons.
questions.explanation: Mass = 5 + 6 = 11 units (electrons are too light to count). The atom has no overall charge, so it has 5 electrons to balance the 5 protons.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Example data: atom A has 6 protons and 6 neutrons. Atom B has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Atom C has 8 protons and 8 neutrons. Which two atoms are the same element?
options: A and C
B and C
A and B
All three are the same element
questions.explanation: The number of protons decides the element. A and B both have 6 protons, so both are carbon, even though they have different numbers of neutrons. C has 8 protons, so it is oxygen.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: Example: a class made models of atoms with no overall charge. Helium: 2 protons, 2 neutrons, 2 electrons. Carbon: 6, 6, 6. Oxygen: 8 protons, 8 neutrons, 6 electrons. Lithium: 3, 4, 3. Nitrogen: 7 protons, 7 neutrons, 8 electrons. Which models have a mistake? Choose all that are right.
options: helium
carbon
oxygen
lithium
nitrogen
questions.explanation: An atom with no overall charge has the same number of electrons as protons. Oxygen has 8 protons but only 6 electrons, and nitrogen has 7 protons but 8 electrons, so both models are wrong.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: In 1911 Rutherford fired tiny particles at a thin sheet of gold. Most went straight through, but a few bounced back. What did this show?
options: Atoms are solid balls with no gaps.
Atoms are mostly empty space with a tiny, heavy centre.
Electrons are heavier than protons.
Gold is not made of atoms.
questions.explanation: Most particles passed through the empty space, but a few hit the tiny, heavy nucleus and bounced back. If atoms were solid balls, more particles would have bounced back.

questions.title: Atoms and Their Structure
questions.stem: An atom contains charged particles, but the atom as a whole has no charge. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: It has the same number of positive protons and negative electrons, so the charges cancel out.
questions.explanation: Each positive proton is balanced by one negative electron. The neutrons have no charge, so the atom has no overall charge.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: A force is…
options: a kind of energy
a type of matter
a push or a pull
a measure of speed
questions.explanation: A force is a push or a pull. We cannot see forces, but we can see what they do: start, stop, speed up, slow down, change direction or change shape.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Sort these into mass (measured in kg) or weight and force (measured in N).
items: the amount of matter in a bag of rice
the number shown by a balance
the pull of gravity on a mango
questions.explanation: Mass is how much matter something has and is measured in kilograms with a balance. Weight is the pull of gravity, a force, so it is measured in newtons with a forcemeter.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Sort these forces into contact forces or non-contact forces.
questions.explanation: Contact forces need the objects to touch. Gravity and magnetic force act at a distance: gravity pulls a mango down from a tree without touching it.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Match each event to the force at work.
pairs: a coconut falls from a palm
a rickshaw's brakes slow its wheels
the string of a flying kite is pulled tight
a boat floats on the river
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls things down, friction slows things that rub, tension is the pull in a stretched string, and upthrust is water pushing up on an object.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Mass is measured in ___ and weight is measured in ___.
questions.explanation: Mass is measured in kilograms (kg). Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons (N).

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: An astronaut has a smaller mass on the Moon than on Earth.
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter, so it stays the same. Her weight is smaller on the Moon because the Moon's gravity pulls less.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: On Earth, an object with a mass of 1 kg has a weight of about…
options: 1 N
6 N
questions.explanation: On Earth, each kilogram has a weight of about 10 newtons.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: A football rolls across grass and slowly stops. Which is the best explanation?
options: The football runs out of force.
Friction from the grass slows it down.
Gravity pulls it backwards.
The grass pushes it up.
questions.explanation: A moving object keeps moving in a straight line unless a force acts on it. Friction between the ball and the grass is the force that stops it.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Match each example to the law of motion it shows.
pairs: a still football stays still until it is kicked
things keep doing what they are doing
a heavy cart needs a bigger push than a light one
a rocket pushes gas down and the gas pushes the rocket up
every push has a push back
questions.explanation: Law 1: things keep doing what they are doing unless a force acts. Law 2: a bigger force makes a bigger change. Law 3: every push has a push back.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: A rickshaw could stop easily without any friction between its tyres and the road.
questions.explanation: Brakes and tyres work because of friction. Without friction, the rickshaw would keep sliding and moving, just as the first law of motion says.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Which of these things can friction do? Choose all that are right.
options: slow down a moving object
help shoes grip the ground
make rubbing surfaces warm
make a still object start moving by itself
make objects heavier
questions.explanation: Friction slows moving things, lets us grip the ground without slipping, and turns movement energy into heat. It cannot start motion on its own or change weight.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Why do people spread sand or gravel on a slippery, muddy path in the monsoon?
questions.model_answer: Sand and gravel increase the friction, so feet and tyres grip the path and do not slip.
questions.explanation: Mud is very smooth, so there is little friction. A rough layer of sand or gravel gives more friction, so people and tyres can grip.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Read the forcemeter. What force does it show?
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter with a scale from 0 to 10 newtons. The pointer is at 4.
options: 3 N
5 N
4 N
6 N
questions.explanation: The pointer is at the 4 on the scale, so the force is 4 newtons. The bigger the pull, the more the spring inside stretches.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Mina hangs a bag of rice on the forcemeter. It reads as shown. On Earth, 1 kg weighs about 10 N. About what is the mass of the rice?
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter with a scale from 0 to 10 newtons. The pointer is at 7.
options: 7 kg
0.7 kg
70 kg
1 kg
questions.explanation: The reading is 7 N, which is the weight. Dividing by 10 N for each kilogram gives a mass of about 0.7 kg.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Look at the picture. Which labelled force acts against the pull and slows the box?
questions.image_alt: A box on the floor with four arrows: pull to the right, friction to the left, weight (gravity) down and support from the floor up.
options: weight (gravity)
pull
support from the floor
friction
questions.explanation: Friction acts in the opposite direction to the movement, where the box rubs on the floor. It is shown by the arrow pointing to the left.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Look at the picture. Which of these forces acts on the box without touching it?
questions.image_alt: A box on the floor with four arrows: pull to the right, friction to the left, weight (gravity) down and support from the floor up.
options: weight (gravity)
friction
support from the floor
pull
questions.explanation: Gravity is a non-contact force: it pulls the box down towards the Earth at a distance. The pull, friction and the support from the floor all need contact.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Match each picture to the force that is acting.
pairs: upthrust holds it up on the water
magnetic force acts at a distance
questions.explanation: Air resistance is friction from the air, upthrust is the push of water or air upwards, a magnet pulls without touching, and a stretched string pulls with tension.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Example tug-of-war (dori tana): in round 2, Team Shapla pulls with 900 N and Team Doel with 750 N. The rope moves towards Team ___, and the difference in force is ___ N.
questions.explanation: The team that pulls harder wins. The unbalanced force is 900 − 750 = 150 N towards Shapla. If both teams pulled 800 N, the forces would be balanced and the rope would not move.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Kabaddi players play barefoot and must grip the ground to push off and turn. Which surfaces would give good grip? Choose all that are right.
options: dry soil
a thick rubber mat
polished smooth tiles
a wet plastic sheet
a rough jute mat
questions.explanation: Rough surfaces such as soil and mats have a lot of friction, so feet grip. Smooth or wet surfaces have little friction, so players would slip.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: A boatman pushes the water backwards with his oar, and the boat moves forwards. Which is the best explanation?
options: The oar pulls the boat forwards through the air.
The water pushes back on the oar, so the boat moves forwards.
Gravity pulls the boat along the river.
The boat moves because it has no mass.
questions.explanation: This is the third law of motion: every push has a push back. When the oar pushes the water backwards, the water pushes the oar, and so the boat, forwards.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Racing bicycles have a smooth, narrow shape. How does this help a cyclist?
options: It reduces air resistance, so the bike can go faster.
It increases air resistance.
It makes the bike heavier.
It makes gravity weaker.
questions.explanation: Air resistance is friction from the air. A shape that cuts through the air has less air resistance, so the cyclist is slowed down less.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Put the steps in order for a carrom shot.
sequence: The striker is flicked and moves across the board.
The striker hits a coin.
Movement energy passes from the striker to the coin.
The striker slows down.
The coin moves off.
questions.explanation: Moving things have movement (kinetic) energy. When the striker hits the coin, some of its energy passes to the coin, so the striker slows and the coin moves.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: In the simulation, with one small puller on the left and one large puller on the right, the cart moves towards the ___ when you press Go.

sim.task: Open Forces and Motion: Basics and choose the Net Force screen. Put one small puller on the left (blue) rope and one large puller on the right (red) rope. Press Go and watch the cart.

questions.explanation: The bigger total pull wins, so the cart moves towards the large puller on the right. If the pulls were equal, the forces would be balanced and the cart would not move.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: In the simulation, with friction set to none, what does the crate do after you stop pushing?

sim.task: Open Forces and Motion: Basics and choose the Friction screen. Set the friction slider to none. Use the applied-force slider to push the crate until it is moving, then set the applied force back to zero and watch the crate.

options: It stops at once.
It slows down slowly and stops.
It speeds up more and more.
It keeps moving at the same speed.
questions.explanation: With no friction there is no force to slow the crate, so it keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line. This is the first law of motion. Try again with lots of friction to see it stop.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens as you keep rubbing the top book across the bottom book?

sim.task: Open Friction. Drag the top book back and forth across the bottom book for a while. Watch the atoms and the thermometer.

options: Nothing changes.
The thermometer reading goes down.
The thermometer reading goes up and the atoms jiggle faster.
The books get heavier.
questions.explanation: Friction turns movement energy into heat. The atoms jiggle faster, so the surfaces get warmer. This is why your hands feel warm when you rub them together.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Class 4D rolled a toy car down a ramp onto four surfaces (example results, mean of three tries): tiles 160 cm, wood 120 cm, carpet 50 cm, grass 25 cm. Put the surfaces in order from the least friction to the most friction.
sequence: tiles (160 cm)
wood (120 cm)
carpet (50 cm)
grass (25 cm)
questions.explanation: The more friction a surface has, the sooner the car stops. The shortest distance, on grass, means the most friction, and the longest distance, on tiles, means the least.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Example tug-of-war results, in newtons. In which rounds are the forces unbalanced, so that the rope moves? Choose all that are right.
options: Round 1: Shapla 800 N, Doel 800 N
Round 2: Shapla 900 N, Doel 750 N
Round 3: Shapla 700 N, Doel 850 N
Round 4: Shapla 600 N, Doel 600 N
Round 5: Shapla 1000 N, Doel 950 N
questions.explanation: Forces are unbalanced when the two pulls are different, even if the difference is small. Rounds 1 and 4 have equal pulls, so the forces are balanced and the rope does not move.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg. On Earth her weight is about 600 N. The Moon's gravity is about 6 times weaker. What are her mass and weight on the Moon?
options: 10 kg and 100 N
60 kg and 100 N
60 kg and 600 N
10 kg and 600 N
questions.explanation: Her mass stays 60 kg because the amount of matter does not change. Her weight is 600 N ÷ 6 = 100 N because gravity is weaker.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: A rickshaw puller pushes an empty van and then the same van loaded with sacks, using the same force each time. Which one speeds up more slowly? Explain why.
questions.model_answer: The loaded van speeds up more slowly, because it has more mass, so the same force makes a smaller change in its speed.
questions.explanation: A bigger mass needs a bigger force to change its speed by the same amount. With the same force, the heavier van changes speed more slowly.

questions.title: Forces and Motion
questions.stem: Joy tests how far a toy car rolls on different surfaces. For the sandpaper she lets the car go from higher up the ramp than for the tiles. What is wrong?
options: She changed the start height as well as the surface, so the test is not fair.
She should have used a heavier car on the sandpaper.
Nothing is wrong, because a higher start makes the test fairer.
She should have used a different ramp for each surface.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing is changed, here the surface. The car, ramp, slope and starting point must stay the same, otherwise we cannot tell what caused the difference in distance.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Which feature helps a duck to float on water?
options: bones that are very heavy
a thick shell on its back
feathers that trap air
a tail as heavy as a stone
questions.explanation: A duck's oily, waterproof feathers trap air, which makes it light for its size. Its webbed feet help it paddle.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Match each living thing to the feature that helps it float or fly.
pairs: an air bag called a swim bladder
questions.explanation: Air makes living things light for their size. Ducks, fish and water hyacinth use air to float, and birds have light hollow bones to fly.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Predict: will each thing float or sink in water? Sort them.
questions.explanation: Things that are light for their size, like wood, leaves and wax, float. Things that are heavy for their size, like stone and metal, sink.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: The upward push of water on an object is called ___.
questions.explanation: Upthrust, also called buoyancy, is the push of water upwards on an object that is in it. It works against the object's weight.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: The four forces of flight are lift, weight, thrust and ___.
questions.explanation: Drag is air resistance. It pulls a flying thing backwards, in the opposite direction to thrust.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: A steel ship floats because it is hollow and full of air, so the ship as a whole is light for its size.
questions.explanation: Solid steel sinks, but a ship's hollow shape displaces a lot of water. This gives enough upthrust to hold up its weight.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: For an aeroplane to take off, which two things must be true?
options: Weight is bigger than lift, and thrust is bigger than drag.
Lift, weight, thrust and drag are all exactly equal.
Lift is bigger than weight, and drag is bigger than thrust.
Lift is bigger than weight, and thrust is bigger than drag.
questions.explanation: To rise, lift must be bigger than weight. To speed up on the runway, thrust must be bigger than drag. When the forces are balanced the plane flies level at a steady speed.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Why does a block of wood float?
options: It is light for its size.
The water pulls it up.
It has no weight.
It is very, very big.
questions.explanation: Wood is light for its size, so it is not very dense. The upthrust from the water can balance its weight, so it floats. A stone is heavy for its size, so it sinks.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Which of these are properties of air? Choose all that are right.
options: Air takes up space.
Air can be squashed into a tyre.
Air has mass.
Air never pushes on anything.
Air cannot move.
questions.explanation: Air takes up space, has mass and can be squashed. Air also pushes on things (air pressure) and moves as wind.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a boat floats.
sequence: The boat pushes some water out of the way (displaces it).
The water pushes back up on the boat.
This upward push is called upthrust.
If the upthrust is as big as the weight, the boat floats.
questions.explanation: A floating object displaces water, and the water pushes back with upthrust. The object floats when the upthrust can become as big as its weight.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Why does a life jacket help you to float?
questions.model_answer: A life jacket is full of air or light foam, so you are less dense overall and the water can push you up enough to float.
questions.explanation: A life jacket works like a duck's feathers: it traps air or light foam. This makes you light for your size, so the upthrust can hold you up.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Match each force of flight to what it does.
questions.explanation: Lift opposes weight, and thrust opposes drag. Weight is the pull of gravity and drag is air resistance.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: A stone sinks because its weight is bigger than the upthrust from the water.
questions.explanation: If the weight is bigger than the biggest upthrust the water can give, the object sinks. A stone is heavy for its size, so the upthrust cannot hold it up.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: The picture shows an aeroplane flying to the right. Which force comes from the engines pushing the plane forward?
questions.image_alt: An aeroplane with four force arrows: lift up, weight down, thrust forward and drag backward.
options: lift
thrust
weight
drag
questions.explanation: Thrust pushes the plane forward and comes from the engines. A bird makes thrust by flapping its wings.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: The plane in the picture is flying level at a steady speed. What does this tell you about the arrows?
questions.image_alt: An aeroplane with four force arrows: lift up, weight down, thrust forward and drag backward.
options: Lift is bigger than weight, and thrust equals drag.
Weight is bigger than lift, and thrust equals drag.
Lift equals weight, and thrust equals drag.
Lift equals weight, and drag is bigger than thrust.
questions.explanation: Level flight at a steady speed means the forces are balanced: lift equals weight, so the plane does not climb or fall, and thrust equals drag, so it does not speed up or slow down.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Look at the pictures. Sort them into things that float on water and things that fly in the air.
questions.explanation: Boats and coconuts rest on the water, held up by upthrust. Eagles, aeroplanes, kites and balloons are held up in the air by lift or by air.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: People have copied nature. Match each invention in the picture to the living thing it copies.
pairs: a fluffy seed drifting on the wind
a hollow coconut floating on water
an eagle soaring on the wind
questions.explanation: Aeroplane wings are curved like a bird's, a parachute catches air like a fluffy seed, boats have wide hollow hulls, and kites use the wind like soaring eagles.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Which of these has oily, waterproof feathers and webbed feet to help it float and paddle?
questions.explanation: A duck's oily feathers trap air and its webbed feet push the water back. Eagles, bats and butterflies are built for flying, not for floating.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Before Eid, a launch that is allowed to carry 300 people sets off with far more. Why is this more likely to make it sink?
options: Upthrust rises more than its weight does.
Its hull gets lighter as people climb aboard.
The water gets denser around the hull.
Its weight rises, so it sits lower and waves wash in.
questions.explanation: Every passenger adds weight, so the boat sits lower in the water. Waves can then wash over the side, and in a storm the boat can capsize.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Example data: a launch is allowed to carry 300 passengers. On trip C it carried 420 passengers, which is ___ more than allowed.
questions.explanation: 420 − 300 = 120 passengers too many. Overloading breaks the safety rules because it makes the boat sit too low in the water.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: A boatman sees that the water has reached the load line painted on the side of his boat. He says: 'The boat is carrying too much.' Is he right?
questions.explanation: A load line shows how low a boat may safely sit. If the water reaches it, the boat is carrying too much and should not leave.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: On Shakrain in Old Dhaka, the wind gives a kite an upward force. What is this force called?
options: thrust
lift
weight
drag
questions.explanation: Lift is the upward force on a flyer. Kite fliers use the wind to give lift and the tension in the string to steer.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: A sky-diver's parachute has a very big canopy. How does that help her land safely?
options: It cuts her weight a lot, so she falls more slowly.
It switches gravity off for as long as she falls.
It adds thrust that pushes her upwards and forwards.
It catches air, so drag is big and she falls slowly.
questions.explanation: A big canopy catches lots of air, which makes a big drag (air resistance) force. Gravity still pulls her down, but the drag slows the fall.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Priya's class is designing a foil boat to carry as many marbles as possible. Which changes would help? Choose all that are right.
options: make the base wider
raise the sides a little
spread the marbles evenly
put all the marbles at one end
crumple the foil into a small ball
questions.explanation: A wide base displaces more water, so there is more upthrust. Higher sides keep water out, and spreading the load keeps the boat balanced. A crumpled ball displaces little water and sinks.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: In the simulation, when a block goes into the water, the water level ___ because the block pushes water out of the way.

sim.task: Open Buoyancy Basics. Drop a block into the pool and watch the water level in the pool.

questions.explanation: The block displaces water, which pushes the water level up. The water that is pushed aside is what pushes back with upthrust.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: In the simulation, blocks that are light for their size float, and blocks that are heavy for their size sink.

sim.task: Open Buoyancy Basics. Drop blocks of different materials into the pool one at a time. Watch which float and which sink, and look at the mass and volume of each block.

questions.explanation: Density tells us how heavy something is for its size. Blocks that are less dense than the liquid float, and denser blocks sink.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Class 4A made foil boats from equal 20 cm squares of foil and added marbles until each sank (example results): flat raft 6, tall narrow 9, wide low tray 24, canoe 15. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Boat shape made no difference to how many it held.
Boat shape changed how many marbles it could hold.
The tall narrow boat held the most marbles.
The flat raft held the most marbles of all four.
questions.explanation: The results range from 6 to 24 marbles with the same amount of foil, so shape matters. The wide low tray held the most because it displaces the most water.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: A ball of clay sinks, but the same clay shaped into a bowl floats. Which statements help to explain this? Choose all that are right.
options: The bowl displaces much more water.
The bowl's upthrust can be as big as its weight.
The clay's mass changed when it was shaped.
The bowl is full of air, so it is light for its size overall.
Clay gets lighter when it is wet.
questions.explanation: The mass of clay is the same, but as a bowl it pushes aside more water and holds air. The upthrust grows until it can match the weight, so the bowl floats.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: Example forces on a plane: lift 50 000 N, weight 40 000 N, thrust 20 000 N and drag 20 000 N. Which statement is right?
options: It rises, because lift is bigger than weight.
It speeds up, because thrust equals drag.
It slows down, because thrust equals drag.
It sinks, because lift is bigger than weight.
questions.explanation: Lift is 10 000 N bigger than weight, so the plane rises. Thrust equals drag, so its forward speed stays steady.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: A steel nail sinks, but a huge steel ship floats. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: The ship is hollow and full of air, so it is light for its size and displaces a lot of water, which gives enough upthrust to hold up its weight. The solid nail is too dense.
questions.explanation: What matters is the shape, not just the material. The hollow ship pushes aside so much water that the upthrust equals its weight. The small solid nail displaces too little water.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: What do we call a complete path that electricity flows round?
options: a circuit
a switch
a conductor
an insulator
questions.explanation: A circuit is a complete path with no gaps. Electricity flows from one end of the cell, through the wires and components, and back to the other end.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Match each circuit part to its job.
questions.explanation: Scientists give each component a job and a symbol. The cell is the energy store; the lamp, buzzer and motor use the energy; the switch controls the circuit.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: What happens to the lamp in a series circuit when you make each change?
items: add a second lamp in the same loop
take one wire out of the loop
questions.explanation: More cells push harder, so the lamp is brighter. A second lamp shares the push, and a longer wire lets less electricity through, so the lamp is dimmer. Any gap stops the electricity completely.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Electricity can flow round a circuit that has a gap in it.
questions.explanation: Electricity needs a complete loop. A gap, such as an open switch or a loose wire, makes the lamp go out.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Materials that let electricity flow through them are called ___. Materials that do not let it flow are called ___.
questions.explanation: Most metals are conductors. Plastic, rubber, wood and glass are insulators.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Why is the inside of an electric cable made of copper?
options: Copper stops shocks reaching our hands.
Copper is a good insulator for wires.
Copper is a magnetic material.
Copper is an excellent conductor.
questions.explanation: Copper lets electricity flow very easily. It is the plastic cover, not the copper, that stops electricity reaching our hands.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which objects would make the bulb light if you joined the gap with them? Choose all that are right.
options: a steel key
a plastic straw
aluminium foil
a wooden spoon
a copper coin
a rubber band
questions.explanation: Steel, aluminium and copper are metals, so they conduct and complete the circuit. Plastic, wood and rubber are insulators, so the gap stays.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to find out how wire length changes the brightness of a bulb.
sequence: Build a circuit with a cell, a bulb and a long thin wire with a crocodile clip.
Clip at 10 cm and measure the brightness with a light meter.
Move the clip to 20 cm and measure again, then 30, 40 and 50 cm.
Draw a line graph of brightness against wire length.
Describe the pattern in the graph.
questions.explanation: First set up the circuit, then take the measurements, then draw the graph, and last describe the pattern you see.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: A ___ opens or closes a gap in a circuit, and a ___ cuts off the electricity if too much flows.
questions.explanation: A switch lets us turn things on and off. Fuses and circuit breakers are safety switches that stop wires getting hot and starting a fire.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Why is an electric cable made with copper wire inside and a plastic cover outside?
questions.model_answer: Copper conducts electricity well, and the plastic is an insulator that keeps the electricity in and protects us from shocks.
questions.explanation: The copper lets electricity flow along the cable. The plastic does not let it flow, so people who touch the cable stay safe.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: A fuse or circuit breaker switches off the electricity if too much flows, before the wires get hot.
questions.explanation: Fuses and circuit breakers are safety switches. Without them, overheated wires could start a fire.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: In 2000, about 32 out of every 100 homes in Bangladesh had electricity. In 2020 it was about 96 out of 100. The rise was ___ homes out of 100.
questions.explanation: 96 - 32 = 64. The figures are approximate, from World Bank data on access to electricity.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Why is the lamp off in this circuit?
questions.image_alt: A circuit with a cell, a lamp and an open switch; the lamp is off.
options: The lamp is too close to the cell.
The wires are the wrong colour.
The switch is open, so there is a gap.
The cell is too small to push electricity.
questions.explanation: An open switch is a gap in the loop. Electricity cannot flow round, so the lamp stays off. Closing the switch would complete the circuit.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Compare this circuit with one that has the same cell and only one lamp. What is different about the lamps here?
questions.image_alt: A circuit with one cell and two lamps in one loop. Both lamps are on.
options: Each lamp is brighter.
Each lamp is dimmer.
Both lamps are the same brightness as one lamp alone.
Only the first lamp lights.
questions.explanation: The cell has to push electricity through two lamps, so it is shared. Each lamp gets less and looks dimmer than a single lamp.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: This model shows tiny particles moving round a circuit. What does it tell us?
questions.image_alt: Tiny particles flowing round a complete circuit loop.
options: They are used up in the lamp.
They flow from the cell to the lamp and stop.
They stay inside the cell.
They flow all the way round the complete loop.
questions.explanation: In a circuit the flow goes all the way round. The lamp changes the energy into light, but the flow itself is not used up.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Sort these pictures into conductors and insulators.
questions.explanation: Keys, coins and steel paper clips are made of metal, so they conduct. Plastic, glass and wood are insulators.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Match each picture to its job.
pairs: tells drivers when to stop and go
moves air to keep us cool
gives light to read at night
charges from a plug or solar panel
questions.explanation: Electrical systems are in homes, schools and the community. Each has a source, wires and a part that does a job.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Tuli has just washed her hands and they are wet. She needs to plug in her phone charger. What should she do?
options: Plug it in quickly while her hands are wet.
Dry her hands well first.
Wrap a wet cloth round the plug.
Push the plug in with a metal spoon.
questions.explanation: Water can conduct electricity, so wet hands near a socket can give a dangerous shock. Always dry your hands first and never push a metal object into a socket.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Raju's kite gets caught on a power line. What should he do?
options: Climb the pole to reach it.
Pull the string hard to get it down.
Leave it there and tell an adult.
Throw a stick at the wire.
questions.explanation: Power lines carry very strong electricity, and a wet string or stick can let it travel down to you. Never touch the kite and always tell an adult.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Lina plugs a fan, a TV, a heater and three chargers into one socket with an adaptor. Why is this dangerous?
options: Too much electricity can overheat the wires and start a fire.
The electricity will stop flowing to every device.
The electricity will leak out of the unused holes.
The devices will all run too fast.
questions.explanation: Each device draws electricity. If too much flows through one socket the wires get hot, which can cause a fire. Use fewer plugs in each socket.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: A cable has a cracked plastic cover and the copper wire is showing. Anika says it is safe to keep using it if she does not touch the wire. Is she right?
questions.explanation: Bare copper can give a deadly shock if anything touches it, and it can start a fire. A damaged cable must be replaced by an adult.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Nadia's class wants to save electricity at school. Which actions would help? Choose all that are right.
options: switch off fans and lights at break
use LED bulbs
leave the computers on all night
unplug chargers when they are not needed
run the fans in empty rooms
questions.explanation: Using less electricity, or using it more efficiently, saves energy. Leaving things on when nobody uses them wastes it.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to use a hair dryer with wet hands in a bathroom?
questions.model_answer: Water that is dirty or salty can conduct electricity, so electricity could flow through your body and give a dangerous shock.
questions.explanation: Normal tap water has dissolved salts, so it conducts. Wet skin lets electricity pass into your body, which can be deadly.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the bulb when you open the switch?

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit. Drag a battery, a light bulb, a switch and wires onto the board to make one complete loop. Close the switch and watch the bulb. Then open the switch.

options: The bulb gets brighter.
The bulb gets a little dimmer.
The bulb stays lit.
The bulb goes out.
questions.explanation: Opening the switch makes a gap in the loop, so no electricity flows and the bulb goes out. Closing it lights the bulb again.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: In the simulation, which objects made the bulb light when you put them in the circuit? Choose all that are right.

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit and choose the Lab screen. Build a loop with a battery and a bulb, leaving a gap. Put each object in the gap one at a time: coin, paper clip, eraser, dollar bill. Watch the bulb each time.

options: coin
paper clip
eraser
dollar bill
questions.explanation: The coin and the paper clip are metal, so they conduct electricity and the bulb lights. The eraser and the paper money are insulators.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: In the simulation, you put a second bulb in the same loop as the first. What happens to the first bulb?

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit. Build a loop with one battery and one bulb and note how bright it is. Then add a second bulb into the same loop (one after the other). Compare the brightness.

options: It gets dimmer.
It gets brighter.
It goes out.
It stays just as bright.
questions.explanation: The battery has to push electricity through both bulbs, so each one is dimmer than a single bulb on its own.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Class 4C measured the brightness of a bulb (in lux) as they made the wire in the circuit longer: 10 cm = 200, 20 cm = 160, 30 cm = 130, 40 cm = 110, 50 cm = 95. What brightness would you expect for 60 cm?
options: about 60 lux
about 110 lux
about 82 lux
about 130 lux
questions.explanation: The bulb gets dimmer as the wire gets longer, but the drops get smaller each time (40, 30, 20, 15). The next drop would be about 12 or 13, giving about 82 lux.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Joy tests whether wire length changes bulb brightness. Test 1 uses a 10 cm wire and a new cell. Test 2 uses a 30 cm wire and an old cell. Why is her test unfair?
options: She measured the brightness with a light meter.
She changed two things, the wire length and the cell.
She used a bulb in both tests.
She tested only two lengths.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing is changed. Joy changed the wire and the cell, so she cannot tell which one made the difference.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Design a burglar alarm for a box. A buzzer must sound when someone opens the lid. Explain how your circuit works.
questions.model_answer: Use a cell, a buzzer and a switch made of two foil strips. When the lid opens the foil strips touch, the circuit is complete, and the buzzer sounds.
questions.explanation: The alarm needs a switch that closes when the lid opens. Closing the switch completes the circuit so electricity flows to the buzzer.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Raju joins one wire from the top of a cell to the base of a bulb. Nothing else touches the bulb or the bottom of the cell. Will the bulb light?
options: Yes, electricity only needs to leave the top of the cell.
Yes, the bulb lights dimly because the wire is short.
No, because a single wire is too short to carry any electricity.
No, there is no complete loop back to the cell.
questions.explanation: A bulb needs a complete loop: out of one end of the cell and back to the other. One wire makes a gap, so electricity cannot flow and the bulb stays off.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Which of these would a magnet attract?
options: a copper wire
an iron nail
an aluminium can
a plastic ruler
questions.explanation: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials. Copper and aluminium are metals but are not magnetic, and plastic is not magnetic either.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Sort these objects into those a magnet attracts and those it does not.
questions.explanation: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are attracted. Aluminium, copper and gold are metals but they are not magnetic.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Match each key word to its meaning.
pairs: the two ends of a magnet, where the force is strongest
a small magnet that swings to point north
the space around a magnet where it has an effect
a magnet made when electricity flows in a coil
questions.explanation: Every magnet has two poles. A compass needle is a small magnet. The field is the space where the magnet can act, and an electromagnet works only while electricity flows.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: All metals are magnetic.
questions.explanation: Only some metals, such as iron, steel and nickel, are magnetic. A magnet will pick up a steel paper clip but not an aluminium can or a copper wire.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: The ends of a magnet are called ___. Like poles ___ each other.
questions.explanation: A magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Like poles (N and N, or S and S) repel; unlike poles attract.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: A magnet can pull a paper clip through a sheet of paper without touching the clip.
questions.explanation: Magnetism is a non-contact force. It acts through the space around the magnet and passes through paper, plastic, water and even your hand.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to make and use an electromagnet.
sequence: Wrap a long wire many times around an iron nail.
Join the ends of the wire to a battery.
Electricity flows through the coil and the nail becomes a magnet.
Pick up some paper clips with the nail.
Disconnect the battery so the clips drop.
questions.explanation: The coil and the nail are made first, then the electricity is switched on. When the electricity is switched off the magnetism disappears and the clips fall.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Which changes would make an electromagnet stronger? Choose all that are right.
options: wrap more coils of wire
use more cells
switch the electricity off
use a wooden stick instead of the iron nail
use a thicker iron core
questions.explanation: More coils, more cells and a thicker iron core all make the magnet stronger. With no electricity there is no magnetism, and wood is not magnetic.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Why can a magnet pick up a steel paper clip but not an aluminium can?
questions.model_answer: Steel contains iron, which is a magnetic material, but aluminium is not magnetic.
questions.explanation: Magnets attract only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Aluminium is a metal but it is not a magnetic material.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Why does a compass needle swing round to point north?
options: Earth behaves like a giant magnet.
The Sun pulls the needle towards the north.
The wind always blows the needle northwards.
The north is the lightest direction to turn.
questions.explanation: A compass needle is a small magnet. The Earth acts like a huge magnet, so the needle lines up with it and points north.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: A big magnet is always stronger than a small magnet.
questions.explanation: Size does not tell you the strength. Some tiny magnets are very strong and some big ones are weak. We test strength by counting paper clips or sheets of paper.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: An electromagnet is made from a coil of ___ wrapped around an iron ___.
questions.explanation: Electricity flowing through the coil of wire turns the iron nail into a magnet. Switch off the electricity and the magnetism disappears.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Mina turns the right-hand magnet in the top pair round, so that two N poles face each other. What will the magnets do?
questions.image_alt: Two pairs of bar magnets. In one pair S faces N and they attract. In the other pair N faces N and they repel.
options: They will pull tightly together.
They will stay exactly where they are.
They will push each other apart.
They will lose their poles for a while.
questions.explanation: Two like poles (N and N) repel. The magnets only attract when a north pole faces a south pole.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Which of these would a magnet pick up?
questions.explanation: A steel paper clip contains iron, so a magnet attracts it. Wood, plastic and glass are not magnetic.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into things a magnet attracts and things it does not.
questions.explanation: Nuts, bolts, pins and needles are made of steel, which contains iron. Feathers, wood and glass are not magnetic.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Match each picture to how it uses magnets or electricity.
pairs: finds the way by pointing north
uses a magnet to make sound
questions.explanation: Compasses, speakers, motors and electric bells all use magnets. Many everyday machines depend on them.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Fishers on the Bay of Bengal use one of these to find north. Which one?
questions.explanation: A compass has a magnetic needle that points north. Torches, keys and candles cannot show direction.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Rafi has a sack of mixed steel cans and aluminium cans for recycling. How can he separate them quickly?
options: Use a magnet to pick up steel cans.
Drop each can into a bucket of water.
Shine a torch on every single can.
Weigh each can on a kitchen scale.
questions.explanation: A magnet attracts the steel cans but not the aluminium ones. This is how recycling plants sort cans.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: A scrap yard crane uses a huge electromagnet, not an ordinary magnet, to move iron and steel. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: An electromagnet can be switched off to drop the scrap where it is needed, but an ordinary magnet would never let go.
questions.explanation: An electromagnet works only while electricity flows. Switch it on to pick up the scrap, and off to drop it onto the truck.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: A fisher is far out on the Bay of Bengal on a cloudy night and cannot see the stars. How can a compass help?
options: It shows how deep the water is below the boat.
It shows which way is north.
It warns him when a cyclone is coming.
It tells him where the fish are swimming.
questions.explanation: The magnetic needle always swings to point north, so the fisher can work out which way to travel even when he cannot see landmarks.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Little Sumi finds a tiny round magnet and puts it in her mouth. This is safe because the magnet is so small.
questions.explanation: Never let small children swallow magnets. They can be very dangerous inside the body. Tell an adult at once.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Tuli's electromagnet lifts only 4 paper clips, but she wants it to lift 10. What should she change?
options: Take one cell away.
Swap the iron nail for a long wooden stick.
Wrap more coils of wire round the nail.
Let the wire hang loosely off the nail.
questions.explanation: More coils make the electromagnet stronger. Fewer cells, a wooden core or a loose wire would make it weaker.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, you add more loops of wire to the coil. What happens to the electromagnet?

sim.task: Open Magnets and Electromagnets and choose the Electromagnet screen. Switch on the battery. Look at the field meter and compass. Then increase the number of loops in the coil and watch again.

options: It gets stronger.
It gets weaker.
It stops working altogether.
Nothing changes.
questions.explanation: More loops make a stronger magnetic field, so the electromagnet can pull harder. This matches what happens with a real coil and nail.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, you reverse the battery of the electromagnet. What happens to its poles?

sim.task: Open Magnets and Electromagnets and choose the Electromagnet screen. Switch on the battery and put the compass near one end of the coil. Note where the needle points. Then reverse the battery and watch the compass.

options: The poles stay exactly where they were.
The north and south poles swap ends.
The magnet disappears.
Both ends become north poles.
questions.explanation: Reversing the battery reverses the direction of the electricity, so the north and south poles swap. You can see it from the compass needle turning round.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, you flip the bar magnet over. What does the compass needle do?

sim.task: Open Magnet and Compass. Move the compass near the bar magnet and watch the needle. Then flip the bar magnet over and watch the needle again.

options: It stays pointing in exactly the same way.
It spins round and round for ever.
It flips round to point the other way.
It disappears.
questions.explanation: The compass needle is a small magnet that lines up with the magnetic field. Flipping the bar magnet flips the field, so the needle turns round.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, with the battery voltage turned down to zero, the coil still works as a strong magnet.

sim.task: Open Magnets and Electromagnets and choose the Electromagnet screen. Set the battery voltage to its highest and look at the field meter. Then turn the voltage down to zero and look again.

questions.explanation: No electricity flowing means no magnetism in an electromagnet. The field meter reads almost zero, and the compass needle is not pulled.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Class 4B counted how many sheets of paper each magnet could pull a paper clip through (mean of 3 tries): bar magnet 13, horseshoe magnet 18, fridge magnet 3, small round magnet 21. Which statement does the data support?
options: The biggest magnet was the strongest.
The horseshoe magnet was the strongest of the four.
The fridge magnet was stronger than the bar magnet.
The small round magnet was the strongest.
questions.explanation: The small round magnet held the clip through the most sheets (21), so it was the strongest. The data do not show that bigger magnets are stronger.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Raju tested an electromagnet (example results): 10 coils lifted 3 clips, 20 coils lifted 6 clips and 30 coils lifted 9 clips. With 40 coils it should lift about ___ clips.
questions.explanation: Every extra 10 coils lifts 3 more clips, so 40 coils should lift 9 + 3 = 12 clips. This is a prediction from the pattern, which we would then test.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: You have a magnet with N and S marked, and a second magnet with no labels. How can you find out which end of the second magnet is its north pole?
questions.model_answer: Bring the N pole of the labelled magnet near one end. If that end repels it, it is a north pole; if it attracts it, it is a south pole.
questions.explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. So an end that pushes the labelled N pole away must also be a north pole.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Raju brings the N pole of his magnet near each end of a mystery bar. One end is attracted and the other end is pushed away. What must the bar be?
options: a plain iron bar
an aluminium bar
a copper bar
a magnet
questions.explanation: Plain iron is attracted at both ends but is never pushed away. Only a magnet can repel another magnet's pole, so the bar is a magnet.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Energy is what makes things…
options: stop, stay still or break
get lost or found
grow heavy or light
work, move or change
questions.explanation: You need energy to run and think, a fan needs it to spin and a lamp needs it to shine. We cannot see energy, but we can see what it does.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Match each example to the form of energy it shows.
questions.explanation: Moving things have kinetic energy. Food and fuels store chemical energy. A stretched band stores energy ready to be used.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Sort these energy sources into those that will run out and those that will not.
questions.explanation: Coal, oil and gas took millions of years to form and will run out. Sunlight, wind, flowing water and biogas can be used again and again.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Energy can be ___ from one form to another, and ___ from one object to another.
questions.explanation: When a fan spins, electrical energy is converted to kinetic energy. When a hot spoon warms your hand, heat is transferred from the spoon to you.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a solar home system gives light.
sequence: Sunlight shines on the solar panel.
The panel changes the light into electrical energy.
Electricity flows along the wires.
The bulb changes the electricity into light and a little heat.
questions.explanation: Energy is tracked step by step: light, then electrical energy, then light again at the bulb, with some heat given off.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: What energy change happens in a solar panel?
options: electrical → light
heat → sound
light → electrical
kinetic → chemical
questions.explanation: A solar panel catches sunlight and changes it into electrical energy. Many families in Bangladesh use solar home systems for lights and phone charging.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Match each device to the energy change it makes.
questions.explanation: Each device changes energy from one form to another, so we can show it as an energy chain.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Rubbing your hands together changes kinetic energy into heat.
questions.explanation: Your hands move (kinetic energy), and friction changes some of that movement into heat, so your hands feel warm.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: A hot spoon warms your hand. What is happening to the heat energy?
options: It is passed on to your hand.
It is made from nothing at all.
It is changed into sound.
It is destroyed when it touches skin.
questions.explanation: Heat energy is transferred (passed on) from the hot spoon to your cooler hand. Energy is not destroyed or created.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Why do we say that almost all of our energy comes from the Sun? Give one example.
questions.model_answer: Plants use the Sun's light to make food, which gives us energy, and coal, oil and gas came from ancient plants.
questions.explanation: Plants store the Sun's energy in food. Fuels such as coal, oil and gas came from ancient plants, and wind and rain are driven by the Sun's heat.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Which action helps to save energy at home?
options: Leave the TV on while you sleep.
Switch off fans in empty rooms.
Use the oldest, hottest bulbs.
Keep the fridge door open longer.
questions.explanation: Using less electricity saves energy. Switching off fans, lights and TVs when nobody is using them is one of the easiest ways.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Which of these have stored (potential) energy? Choose all that are right.
options: a book on a high shelf
a stretched rubber band
water behind a dam
a rolling football
a flowing river
questions.explanation: Stored energy is waiting to be used. A rolling football and a flowing river are moving, so they have kinetic energy.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Some energy is always wasted as ___, which is why a bulb or a motor gets warm.
questions.explanation: No machine turns all its energy into useful work. Some always escapes as heat.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Sort these pictures by the main useful energy they give out.
questions.explanation: Bulbs and torches give out light, speakers and radios give out sound, and fans and cars move. Each one converts energy into a useful form.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Which picture shows a device that changes light from the Sun into electrical energy?
questions.explanation: A solar panel catches sunlight and changes it into electrical energy. A fan, a candle and a loudspeaker do different jobs.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Match each picture to the energy it stores or gives out.
pairs: has kinetic energy in moving air
questions.explanation: Food stores chemical energy, a fire gives out heat and light, a speaker gives out sound, and moving air has kinetic energy.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Put the pictures in order to follow the energy from the Sun to a bicycle ride.
questions.explanation: The Sun's light helps rice grow and stores chemical energy. We eat the rice, and our muscles change the chemical energy into the movement of the bicycle.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Which picture shows a device that changes electrical energy into sound?
questions.explanation: A loudspeaker turns electrical energy into sound. A bulb makes light, a fan makes movement, and a torch changes chemical energy in its cells to light.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: A family in a village makes biogas from cow dung. Why is biogas called a renewable source?
options: It took millions of years to form deep underground.
More gas can be made while the cows keep eating.
It comes from under the ground and is soon used up.
It is made from coal that has been cleaned.
questions.explanation: Cows eat grass and make dung all the time, so new gas can keep being made. Coal, oil and natural gas took millions of years to form and will run out.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: An old filament bulb gets very hot, but an LED bulb stays cool. Which one wastes more energy as heat?
options: both waste exactly the same
the LED bulb
the old filament bulb
neither one wastes any
questions.explanation: Much of the electrical energy in a filament bulb becomes heat instead of light. LEDs give the same light with much less electricity.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Sumi's village home has a small solar panel on the roof that lights her lamp at night. Where does that energy come from?
options: burning coal at the power station
gas from under the ground
the wind turning the panel
the light of the Sun
questions.explanation: The solar panel changes sunlight into electrical energy, which can be stored in a battery for the evening. Sunlight is a renewable source.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: A family burns 15 kg of firewood every week. If a biogas plant replaces all of it, they save ___ kg of wood in a year of 52 weeks.
questions.explanation: 15 × 52 = 780 kg. Biogas also means no smoke in the kitchen and fewer trees cut down.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Why is cooking with biogas healthier for a family than burning wood or dried dung?
questions.model_answer: Biogas burns with a clean flame and makes no smoke, so the family does not breathe smoke that harms their lungs.
questions.explanation: Smoke from wood and dung fills the kitchen and harms the lungs of women and children. Biogas burns cleanly and the leftover slurry makes fertiliser.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: In the simulation you choose the Sun, a solar panel and a light bulb. What is the energy chain?

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Systems screen. Choose the Sun as the energy source, the solar panel as the energy changer and the light bulb as the energy user. Watch the energy symbols.

options: electrical → kinetic → heat
chemical → sound → light
light → electrical → light
heat → electrical → sound
questions.explanation: The solar panel changes the Sun's light into electrical energy. The bulb then changes the electricity back into light, with a little heat.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: In the simulation, the cyclist pedals to light a bulb through a generator. Put the energy changes in order.

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Systems screen. Choose the cyclist as the energy source, the generator as the changer and the light bulb as the user. Watch the energy symbols as the cyclist pedals.

sequence: chemical energy in the cyclist's body
kinetic energy of the pedalling cyclist
electrical energy from the generator
light from the bulb
questions.explanation: The cyclist's food energy (chemical) becomes movement (kinetic). The generator turns movement into electricity, and the bulb turns electricity into light.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: In the simulation, where does the skater have the most kinetic energy (movement energy)?

sim.task: Open Energy Skate Park Basics and choose the Intro screen. Switch on the energy bar graph. Release the skater from the top of the ramp and watch the bars as the skater rolls down.

options: at the bottom of the ramp
at the top, before letting go
at the same level on both sides
only when the skater is stopped
questions.explanation: As the skater rolls down, stored energy changes to kinetic energy. The kinetic energy is greatest at the bottom, where the skater moves fastest.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Class 4A pulled a rubber band back by 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 cm. A toy car travelled 40, 85, 130, 170 and 210 cm. About how far would the car go for a pull of 12 cm?
options: about 190 cm
about 250 cm
about 420 cm
about 300 cm
questions.explanation: Each extra 2 cm of pull adds about 40 to 45 cm, so 12 cm gives about 210 + 40 = 250 cm. A more stretched band stores more energy, which becomes more kinetic energy.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: A bouncing ball rises a little lower after each bounce until it stops. Where does the ball's lost movement energy go?
options: It disappears completely.
It changes into heat and sound.
It goes into the Sun.
It is stored in the air as light.
questions.explanation: Energy is never destroyed, only changed. Each bounce turns some movement energy into heat and sound in the ball and the floor.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: 'Energy is never used up, it only changes form.' Use a bicycle that slows down and stops when you stop pedalling to explain this.
questions.model_answer: The bicycle's kinetic energy is not destroyed. Friction and air resistance change it into heat, and a little sound, in the tyres, brakes and air.
questions.explanation: When you stop pedalling, friction and air resistance slowly turn the kinetic energy into heat. The energy has changed form, not vanished.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: An old bulb takes in 100 units of electrical energy (example numbers) and gives out only 10 units as light. The other ___ units are wasted, mostly as heat.
